#3605. These Are the Best Early Black Friday Deals on Soundbars From Sony, Bose, Samsung, and LG

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Upgrading your TV's sound doesn't necessarily mean spending a fortune on a full home theater setup, especially with early Black Friday deals bringing substantial discounts on soundbars and audio systems from Sony, Bose, Samsung, and LG. Sony has some of the biggest price cuts, with savings of up to 32% across select Bravia Theater models, including more than $700 off its premium Theater Trio system.

Samsung's Dolby Atmos soundbars are also discounted by as much as $400, while Bose and LG have more affordable options for anyone looking to improve dialogue clarity, add some bass, or enjoy surround sound without a complicated setup. Whether you're shopping for a compact speaker for a bedroom TV or a more immersive system for movie nights, here are the deals worth considering.

For anyone building a premium home theater around a large TV, the Sony Bravia Theater Trio is down to $1,498 from $2,199.99, saving you $701.99, or roughly 32%. Unlike a conventional soundbar, the Trio uses three separate front speakers for the left, center, and right channels, helping spread dialogue and effects across a wider soundstage. You can read PCMag’s “excellent” review for more details.

The Sony Bravia Theater Bar 7 is down to $718 from $869 for anyone who wants a single soundbar under the TV. Its nine speakers include upward- and side-firing drivers that widen the soundstage and give Dolby Atmos some height, but there’s no subwoofer, so the now $898 Bar 7 with a wireless sub bundle (down from $1,099.99) might be the better pick for deeper bass.

Moving down Sony's lineup, the Bravia Theater Bar 6 is $548, down from $699.99, and pairs a 3.1.2-channel soundbar with a wireless subwoofer and upward-firing speakers for Dolby Atmos height effects. Spending $100 more gets you the Bravia Theater System 6, now $648 from $799.99, which adds rear speakers in a 5.1-channel setup for movies and games where sound moves behind you.

For a more affordable upgrade, the Sony Bravia Theater Bar 5 is down to $278 from $349.99, saving you nearly $72. It's a 3.1-channel system with a dedicated center speaker and wireless subwoofer, so dialogue should come through more clearly while music and movie effects get some additional low-end presence.

Sony’s older systems are discounted too, including the HT-S400 at $258, down from $299, which pairs a 2.1-channel soundbar and wireless subwoofer with S-Force Pro Front Surround to widen the sound for everyday TV, sports, and casual movies. The HT-S40R is arguably the better deal at the same $258, down from $329.99, since it adds two rear speakers for a full 5.1-channel setup, though neither model supports Dolby Atmos.

For smaller rooms or for anyone who mainly wants dialogue to come across more clearly, Bose has two compact soundbars on sale: The newer Bose TV Speaker (2nd Gen) is down to $239 from $299, with an updated acoustic design that Bose says improves clarity and overall sound performance. Meanwhile, the original Bose TV Speaker is $199, down from $279, and offers a similarly compact design with a dedicated dialogue mode and adjustable bass.

Samsung’s HW-Q800H is down to $697.99 from $1,097.99, a $400 cut on a 5.1.2-channel Dolby Atmos soundbar with a wireless subwoofer. Its side- and upward-firing speakers help place effects around and above you, while a dedicated center channel keeps dialogue clear during busy action scenes.

For something that takes up less space, the Samsung HW-S60D is $277.99, down from $399.99, and fits seven speakers, including side-firing drivers, into a compact 5.0-channel soundbar. It also supports Dolby Atmos, Adaptive Sound, and a voice enhancement mode, along with Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, AirPlay, and Chromecast for music streaming. That said, it has no upward-firing speakers or subwoofer, so its height effects and bass won’t match that of the Q800H.

If you're looking for a complete surround sound system without spending several hundred dollars, the LG S6FTR is down to $249.99 from $399.99, saving you $150, or roughly 38%. It's a 5.1-channel home theater package with a soundbar, subwoofer, and dedicated rear speakers. That makes it particularly appealing for action movies and games, where directional sound adds to the experience.

The LG S40TR is another affordable option for anyone who wants rear speakers included in the box. It's currently $199.99, down from $279.99, and offers a 4.1-channel arrangement with a wireless subwoofer and two rear speakers. This should give movie soundtracks a greater sense of direction than a basic soundbar, while the subwoofer handles the lower frequencies that smaller TV speakers often struggle to reproduce.

At just under $187, the S60T is the least expensive system in this roundup, pairing a 3.1-channel soundbar with a wireless subwoofer for clearer dialogue and fuller sound than your TV’s speakers. That said, it lacks rear speakers and Dolby Atmos height channels, so it’s better suited to someone who wants a simple, affordable upgrade without filling the room with additional hardware.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

Black Friday used to be bigger for major retailers and more expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was better for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Nowadays, though, the distinction is almost meaningless. Every major retailer will offer sales on both days, and the smart move is to know what you want, do your research, or refer to guides like our Black Friday and Cyber Monday coverage that have done all the vetting for you.

#3604. 44 Years Later, Steven Spielberg's Scariest Movie of All Time Is Officially Free on Streaming

Brian VanHooker is a Pop Culture Writer specializing in Celebrity Interviews and In-Depth Oral Histories in the areas of Comedy, TV, Film, Cartoons, Comic Books, 80s/90s Nostalgia, Fatherhood, Retro Games and Food (especially Pizza). He was the Senior Features Writer at Cracked and a Staff Writer at MEL. He has written for Inverse, Inside Hook, Maxim, Men's Health, Fatherly, SFGate and more. He's the co-creator of the comic book/cartoon Barnum & Elwood and The Tramp, an award-winning comedy pilot starring John O’Hurley. He also hosts a TMNT interview podcast called Turtle Tracks and was once called a “Good Guy” by Mr. T.

Somehow, people remain confused as to who actually directed it

Sometimes, people who make movies don’t get the credit they deserve. Carrie Fisher served as an uncredited script doctor on the 1998 Adam Sandler movie The Wedding Singer, and Quentin Tarantino did an uncredited rewrite of the Saturday Night Live sketch-turned-movie It’s Pat. This is more common with writers than directors, but it can happen to directors, too. For example, Richard Donner, who helmed the 1979 masterpiece Superman, shot much of the sequel Superman II, but was fired partway through the movie. Richard Lester, who replaced him, received full credit. And while the details remain unclear​​​​​​​, there’s a certain 1982 horror film that many speculate was directed by someone other than the person named in the credits​​​​​​​.

Poltergeist, which became available to stream for free on Pluto TV on Nov. 1​​​​​​​, follows ​​​​​​​an ordinary suburban family that begins to experience​​​​​​​ strange things in their home. Furniture and toys move on their own, a glass of milk shatters out of nowhere, and the youngest child in the family, 5-year-old Carol Anne (Heather O'Rourke), begins to communicate with beings through the television. At first, these events are dismissed, but during a thunderstorm one night, a tree outside the windows of the kids’ room crashes in and snatches the boy. Then, a portal opens in their closet, sucking Carol Anne into another dimension. With help from some paranormal investigators, the family tries everything to bring her back.​​​​​​​

The credited director of Poltergeist​​​​​​​ is Tobe Hooper, who is best known for directing The Texas Chainsaw Massacre and other gruesome horror films, as well as a couple of sci-fi horror films, including Lifeforce​​​​​​​. The movie was also produced by Steven Spielberg, and to this day, there’s an ongoing debate about which of the two men was the real director.

The contradictions between the two parties begin as far back as the very beginning of production. Originally, after Close Encounters of the Third Kind, Spielberg wanted to do a sci-fi horror film called Night Skies, which followed a handful of aliens who land on Earth and terrorize a family​​​​​​​. Eventually, Spielberg reworked that idea into the heartwarming E.T., which was much more suitable to his sensibilities. Still, he wasn’t entirely cool with letting go of Night Skies, so he brought in director Tobe Hooper to maybe direct it. Some say Hooper changed Night Skies into Poltergeist, substituting ghosts for aliens, while Hooper himself has said he shot down Night Skies and came in with the entirely original idea of Poltergeist, which he’d been working on for years.

Regardless, Poltergeist went into production with Hooper at the helm while Spielberg was continuing work on E.T. Yet Spielberg was also on set a lot for Poltergeist and seemed to micromanage the production. With Spielberg's vocal, enthusiastic style versus Hooper's quieter approach to directing, it gave the impression of two directors on set.

For example, John Leonetti, who worked as a camera assistant on the movie and is the brother of Poltergeist cinematographer Matthew Leonetti, has said Spielberg was effectively directing the movie​​​​​​​. Meanwhile, stars JoBeth Williams and Craig T. Nelson, who played the parents in the movie, have confirmed that Hooper was the director (while also acknowledging that Spielberg was very hands-on as a producer). Zelda Rubinstein, who played medium Tangina Barrons, said it was a joint venture, but that Spielberg had a bit more control than Hooper.

Contemporary interviews with Spielberg also muddy the picture. He told The Los Angeles Times in 1982: "Tobe isn't what you'd call a take-charge sort of guy. He's just not a strong presence on a movie set. If a question was asked and an answer wasn't immediately forthcoming, I'd jump up and say what we could do. Tobe would nod agreement, and that became the process of the collaboration."

It didn’t help that Poltergeist and E.T. were released just a year apart in 1982 and many took to calling it “Spielberg Summer.” MGM and United Artists also touted Spielberg’s name over Hooper’s in promoting the film. The Directors’ Guild even looked into the matter and determined that the studio had denigrated Hooper’s title; the studio was forced to pay Hooper $15,000.

Then there’s the question of style. Some say the movie’s focus on a suburban family​​​​​​​ and high level of polish point to Spielberg’s direction, as Hooper’s work was scrappier and more horrifying. Then again, Hooper rarely had the kind of budget he had for Poltergeist​​​​​​​. Particularly scary scenes, such as the one in which a paranormal investigator peels off his face and the one in which Williams’ character falls into a muddy pit of bodies, also feel much more like Hooper’s work.​​​​​​​

In truth, the final result is probably the clearest proof that the movie was, indeed, a collaboration. Poltergeist does have an accessible, almost heartwarming family element to it that makes you really care about the characters in the way you would in a great Spielberg film. And there are moments of genuine terror that remind you of Hooper. There’s also a masterful sense of tension in the movie, something that both directors excelled at​​​​​​​, which can be seen in the first half of The Texas Chainsaw Massacre with Hooper at the helm, as well as the first half of Spielberg's Jaws. Perhaps, had they been credited as co-directors, there would be no controversy so many decades later. Regardless, Poltergeist is one of the best films from the 1980s, and it's certain to appeal to fans of both Hooper and Spielberg.

Poltergeist is available on HBO Max and for free on Pluto TV.

#3603. Hexed Might Be A Major Misfire For Disney Animation At The Box Office

Disney has produced many of the best animated movies of all time. They've been doing it longer than anyone else and, arguably, better than anyone else for decades. Unfortunately though, original animation has been a tough sell to audiences in recent years, and Disney's "Hexed" looks like it's going to suffer at the box office as a result of this trend.

"Hexed" is currently eyeing an opening in the $23 million range, per Box Office Theory. That's across the full five-day, Wednesday to Sunday stretch since this movie is opening mid-week for the Thanksgiving holiday. The comedy "Focker In-Law" pits Ben Stiller against Ariana Grande and looks to win the weekend with around $36 million. For what it's worth, earlier tracking (via Deadline) had both movies doing between $40 and $50 million across the five-day stretch.

More than A24's "Club Kid" or or the "Hershey" biopic, also releasing over Thanksgiving, it's "The Hunger Games" that will be a bigger issue for Disney's latest. "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" will be a bigger hit than you realize, doing well over $100 million on opening weekend. That means, in its second frame, it could still easily take number one over Thanksgiving.

Disney's latest centers on an impulsive and unconventional teenage girl named Billie (Hailee Steinfeld) who discovers secret magical abilities which. Once unleashed, they hurtle her out of suburbia and into a vast witch realm called Hexe. Fawn Veerasunthorn and Jason Hand directed the movie, with Josie Trinidad co-directing.

The big issue for "Hexed" is that these movies don't come cheap. We're looking at a budget of at least $150 million, if not much more. Even at $150 million, an opening under $30 million across a robust, long holiday weekend is close to a death sentence. Yes, there are overseas markets to account for and family-friendly movies can have long legs. Even so, the early estimates are rough, to put it kindly.

It's especially disappointing because this feels like the right place on the calendar for the movie. "Moana 2" smashed box office records and led to the biggest Thanksgiving ever in 2024. That eventually became a $1 billion hit for Disney. But that was a sequel to a much-beloved move from the 2010s. Originals, from both Disney Animation and Pixar, have struggled mightily in the 2020s.

Case in point, "Strange World" bombed at the box office in 2022, taking in just $73 million worldwide. "Hexed" doesn't appear to be in such terrible shape but it's not looking good. Disney's "Wish" was also a big disappointment at the box office in 2023, doing $255 million worldwide. Decent for an original movie by today's standards but not nearly good enough to turn a profit.

The only thing Disney can hope for is that word of mouth amongst moviegoers is outstanding, which could give "Hexed" unusually long legs. Or that tracking is just wildly off and the movie actually comes in closer to earlier estimates. Either way, as it stands, this one looks like it just has one too many hurdles to clear.

Disney's "Hexed" hits theaters on November 25, 2026.

Arguably the greatest Christmas franchise of all time is getting its star back. 34 years after 1992's "Home Alone 2: Lost in New York," Macaulay Culkin is set to return as Kevin McCallister in a third movie that will act as a sequel/reboot for the saga.

In July 2026, we got an update on "Home Alone 3" (as we'll call it until further notice) that suggested Culkin's return was more likely than ever, as the actor reportedly paid a visit to the Disney lot where he met with studio head David Greenbaum. Culkin's film would follow an adult Kevin McCallister who's become too focused on work at the expense of his young son. Kevin would then become locked out of his own house with his son still inside before having to break back in and avoid his son's ingenious traps in what is essentially a metaphor for working his way back into his son's heart. Not bad, right? For now, it remains unclear whether this is, in fact, the pitch Disney has greenlit, but it would make sense.

The other films in the saga? Nowhere to be seen. Lord knows the "Home Alone" movies need a major revitalization, and you couldn't do better than Culkin's return in that regard.

#3601. Microsoft Officially Apologized for Yesterday's Outages

If you were having trouble accessing certain services like Microsoft Teams or Outlook, you were not alone. Early Thursday afternoon, many of Microsoft's biggest apps and services were experiencing downtime. According to Downdetector, which tracks user reports of issues with websites and platforms, Microsoft 365, Teams, Copilot, Teams, and OneDrive were all experiencing issues. As of Friday afternoon, Microsoft has restored service to many users, and has officially apologized for the outages.

When I first published this article on Thursday, I couldn't even load Microsoft 365's status page. (I've reported on many service outages, but I can't recall a time when a service's status page was also down.) Even as of Friday afternoon, the page still says "Service degradation on Microsoft 365 (Business or Enterprise)," and Microsoft says the following services may be affected: Exchange Online, Microsoft 365 admin center, Microsoft 365 apps, Microsoft 365 Apps Admin Center, Microsoft 365 Education, Microsoft Copilot 365, Microsoft Defender for Office 365, Microsoft Defender XDR, Microsoft Fabric, Microsoft Graph, Microsoft Intune, Microsoft Planner, Microsoft Power Apps, Microsoft Purview, Microsoft Teams, Microsoft To Do, Power BI, SharePoint Online, Universal Print, and Windows 365.

Looking specifically at Outlook, Microsoft's email service had hundreds of thousands of user reports Thursday afternoon, signaling a major issue somewhere in Microsoft's pipeline. The reports did "slow down" throughout the day, but Downdetector still showed over 50,000 reports coming in every 15 minutes when I checked Thursday afternoon.

While the root cause of the issue was a mystery throughout Thursday's outage, Microsoft confirmed the problem in an apology on Friday. According to the company, "This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI [or] agents. The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions."

Microsoft says it is "deeply sorry" for the disruption to its customers and partners. The company says the fix rolled out slower than some might expect, since it wanted to restore service gradually to evaluate stability at each stage. It also says it will release a full post-incident report once it completes a review.

During the outage, the company had confirmed that some of its infrastructure was experiencing elevated load, which it said was likely contributing to the issues. Microsoft then said it was pausing all deployments and moving traffic from affected infrastructure, and that it found that a number of its servers were unexpectedly unavailable after failing health checks. The company then thought a specific component responsible for processing server health may be the reason the system is failing health checks. Microsoft said an alternative service health check method successfully restarted some of the affected servers. The company was then actively restarting and validating affected servers to bring them back to service.

#3599. Why Maysilee Donner From The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping Looks So Familiar

This article contains spoilers for "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping."

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" adapts the story that fans have been waiting for since 2008, revealing how Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada), future mentor of Katniss Everdeen (Jennifer Lawrence), became the victor of the 50th Hunger Games. Haymitch's games were even more brutal than usual: as a special "quarter quell" game, each of the twelve districts had to offer up four children, not two. (Haymitch ends up in the games after one of the two District 12 boys originally chosen tries to flee and then is shot.)

One of the District 12 kids "reaped" alongside Haymitch is Maysilee Donner (Mckenna Grace), the daughter of a candy shop owning family. A jewelry collector, Maysilee is the original owner of the Mockingjay pin that Katniss eventually comes to wear during the "Hunger Games" trilogy.

Now, this being a prequel where Haymitch's victory (as pyrrhic as it is) is assured, you should go into "Sunrise on the Reaping" knowing Maysilee doesn't walk out of that arena. Grace actually plays two roles in the film, the other being Maysilee's twin sister, Merrilee. Once Haymitch returns, during Maysilee's funeral, he has to see the very same face of the girl he failed.

Viewers, too, might recognize Maysilee and Merrilee's shared face. Mckenna Grace is a prolific young actress with many film and TV (including voiceover) roles to her name. In just the past few years, she appeared in "Five Nights at Freddy's 2" as paranormal activity hunter Lisa, Clara in the Colleen Hoover adaptation "Regretting You," and Hannah Thurman in "Scream 7." Those recent roles only scratch the surface of her acting resume.

Born in 2006, Mckenna Grace is a recently graduated child actress; her first acting role was on the 2012 Disney XD series "Crash and Bernstein." Soon after she had a part on soap opera "The Young and the Restless" from 2013 to 2015 as Faith Newman. Her breakout film role was in 2017 Chris Evans vehicle "Gifted," where she played young math prodigy Mary Adler.

In the late 2010s, Grace found a niche playing child versions of main characters. She played young Tonya Harding in "I, Tonya," young Carol Danvers in "Captain Marvel," a young Sabrina Spellman in one episode of "The Chilling Adventures of Sabrina," and starred in Mike Flanagan's miniseries "The Haunting of Hill House" as a young version of Kate Siegel's character Theo Crain. This means she's played young versions of Margot Robbie, Brie Larson, and Kiernan Shipka. (Grace, who played Paige Swanson on sitcom "Young Sheldon," has said she envisions Reese Witherspoon as the adult version of that character.)

From 2021 to 2022, during Seasons 4 and 5 of "The Handmaid's Tale," Grace played Esther Keyes, the abused teenage wife of a much older man. This role earned her an Emmy nomination for Outstanding Guest Actress in a Drama Series. 2021 was also the year that Grace starred in "Ghostbusters: Afterlife" as Phoebe Spangler, later reprising the role in 2024's "Ghostbusters: Frozen Empire."

One of Grace's voiceover roles was playing a young version of Daphne Blake in the 2020 animated "Scooby Doo!" film "Scoob!" Fresh off of "Sunrise on the Reaping," she's going to play Daphne again, this time in live-action, in the upcoming TV series "Scooby Doo: Origins" due out in 2027.

#3598. 10 Books Like ‘A Court of Thorns and Roses’ You Should Read Next

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Sarah J. Maas’ lush, romance-soaked series A Court of Thorns and Roses has blossomed into a sprawling, complex fantasy series with millions of dedicated fans, and with good reason. A complex heroine who keeps discovering new depths in herself, fascinating supporting characters who shift from antihero to antivillain in unexpected ways, creative and beautifully rendered world-building—the series has it all, while also being unapologetically romantic (and steamy).

The story of a huntress who is kidnapped by a fae prince and brought to the Spring Court as a prisoner, only to become a key player in all that fae drama, ACOTAR is special, but Maas can only write so fast. If you need more books with the same lush feel, here are 10 to get you started.

It’s no shock that one of Sarah J. Maas’ other series would be recommended for fans of A Court of Thorns and Roses, but there’s a specific reason you should jump into her Crescent City series, especially the third book, House of Flame and Shadow. The most recent ACOTAR book, A Court of Splintered Harmony, revealed that the events of House of Flame and Shadow tie directly into the events in Splintered Harmony, particularly with regard to the character of Feyre’s sister, Nesta. In other words, if you read Splintered Harmony and wondered why Nesta was being so weird, there’s a whole other book series you should dig into immediately.

If Feyre’s grit and determination are your favorite aspect of ACOTAR, Julie Kagawa’s Iron Fey series (starting with The Iron King) will be your next obsession. Meghan Chase has never felt ‘normal’ in her life, and she’s been haunted by her father’s disappearance since she was a child. When her brother also vanishes, she goes on a quest for answers, learns that she’s actually the daughter of a faerie king, and finds herself in a magical world that blurs in elements of Shakespeare’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream. Meghan is determined to save her brother (and herself), but a certain ice-cold fae prince captures her attention, even though he’s as dangerous as he is beautiful.

If you’re looking for some serious romance in your fantasy, Jennifer L. Armentrout’s A Blood and Ash series is a must. Poppy was chosen at birth to be the kingdom’s Maiden, isolated and untouched in order to be ready for her Ascension to ensure the land is protected from the evil force that took her family. But it’s a lonely existence—until Hawke is assigned as her sworn protector. Golden-eyed and beautiful, Hawke offers Poppy the connection she’s craved. When chaos erupts around her, Hawke takes the opportunity to spirit Poppy away. But Hawke has a secret, and Poppy is soon in danger of losing both her heart and the favor of the gods themselves.

If you love how A Court of Thorns and Roses takes the “enemies-to-lovers” trope and builds it into a deep, complex mesh of emotions and plot twists, you’ll love Shelby Mahurin’s Serpent & Dove series. When witch Louise le Blanc flees her coven, she takes shelter in the city of Cesarine, where magic is forbidden, and witches are unceremoniously hunted and burned. Louise’s life gets infinitely more complicated, dangerous, and steamy when she’s trapped into an unwanted marriage with Reid Diggory—who happens to be a huntsman of the Church, charged with tracking down and eliminating witches. And then Louise starts to realize that Reid is actually pretty darn hot.

If you’re looking for a romantasy that’s broadly similar to ACOTAR while being its own thing, read A.K. Mulford’s The Five Crowns of Okrith series, starting with The High Mountain Court. Remy is a red witch, which means she’s in hiding and ready to make a run for it if the fae get near. So when a group of fae shows up at her tavern, she makes for the exit—only to be captured by Prince Hale of the Eastern Court. Instead of striking her down, however, Hale asks Remy for help—he needs to locate two ancient magical artifacts created by red witches, and he needs her red magic to find them. Hale promises to set her free and even reunite her with the red witches still living. More importantly, Remy finds Hale irresistible and has a primal urge to stay with him, no matter what the cost.

Looking for a romantasy with a slightly different vibe from ACOTAR? Variety is the spice of life, after all—and The Fourth Wing delivers. Rebecca Yarros’ Empyrean Series made a huge splash when it debuted, and for good reason—it has everything, from a capable, intelligent heroine thrust into a dangerous scenario (in this case, a dragon rider academy where failure can be deadly) and forced to navigate alliances, conspiracies, and her own heart, which is pushing her towards a romance that might be as dangerous as the dragons themselves.

Love the moral complexity of ACOTAR, where everyone has at least a touch of darkness? Check out The Folk of the Air series by Holly Black. When Jude was a child, the father of her half-sister, the faerie Madoc, murdered her parents and took her back to the Faerie world with him. Raised as part of the gentry, Jude lives in a world where her mortal nature is hated and despised, but she battles for her place at court anyway while struggling with her love-hate relationship with her adoptive father and a growing bond with the titular prince, a relationship that is strictly forbidden. Jude is a fierce and extremely morally gray character, and one that fans of Feyre will adore.

Looking for more smart women at the center of beautifully-rendered fantasy stories? You’ll love Princess Lucero-Elisa de Riqueza of Orovalle, star of this series-starter by Rae Carson. Elisa was chosen for “Service” as a baby, when a godstone was placed in her navel by the gods, signaling that she was destined for greatness. But as a young woman, Elisa is self-hating and miserable. She’s never done anything even remotely great, and spends her time isolated, overweight, and reading military strategy books. One day she’s shocked to discover she’s been married off to the king of a distant land on the brink of war—and suddenly all that rage and book learning becomes invaluable as she struggles to survive an unfamiliar court and help her new homeland survive a dangerous onslaught.

If you loved Feyre’s journey as she discovered unknown reservoirs of power and courage inside herself, you should read Leigh Bardugo’s Grishaverse novels, starting with Shadow and Bone. As a child, Alina was tested by the Grisha and found to possess no magical ability. As an adult, she serves as a cartographer in the army. Charged with guiding the Darkling—the most powerful of the Grisha—across the dangerous and terrifying Shadow Fold, Alina is unexpectedly revealed to have incredible powers and is packed off to train with the Grisha. There, she must determine who her friends and enemies are, even while falling under the spell of the charismatic Darkling.

Emilia di Carlo and her sister Vittoria are very different—Emilia is bookish and shy, Vittoria outgoing and brash—but they share a secret: They’re both streghe, and have spent their lives learning to use magic. In this version of Italy, the Malvagi (the seven princes of Hell) haven’t been seen in a long time, but a terrifying accident summons the Prince of Wrath and leaves three witches dead, including Vittoria. Emilia swears to use her power to avenge her sister, but when her revenge is delayed and she’s forced to work with Wrath, unwanted feelings begin to tick up the spice level to an uncomfortable degree.

#3597. MobLand Season 2 Finale Delivers The Show's Most Shocking Death Yet

This article contains spoilers for "MobLand" Season 2, Episode 10, "The Queen is Dead."

Just when you think the Harrigans might catch a break, things blow up in their face. This time, a car literally blew up in the face of Tom Hardy's Harry Da Souza and his daughter, Gina Da Souza (Teddie Allen), during a frenetic "MobLand" Season 2 finale which almost ended without anyone kicking the bucket. In the episode's final moments, however, we witness what is surely the most shocking death in the entire series, when Joanne Froggatt's Jan Da Souza gets blown sky high thanks to Anson Boon's Eddie Harrigan.

"Mobland" started life as a "Ray Donovan" spin-off, with Hardy set to play the English equivalent of Liev Schreiber's fixer — which he still sort of does. But his Harry is much darker, colder, and quietly ruthless. Alan Ritchson once compared playing Jack Reacher to playing an alligator waiting to strike. If that's true, then Hardy's Da Souza is a human nuclear warhead, sitting at the head of a ballistic missile and waiting to reduce the world to ashes. Thus far, despite the many challenges endured by the Harrigans in "MobLand" Season 2, he's managed to maintain his icy exterior. Now that his wife has gone up in flames, however, I get the feeling that reservoir of repressed rage is going to come flooding out in Season 3.

Season 2, Episode 10 has a deceptive title. When I first saw "The Queen is Dead" on the Paramount+ interface, I thought Maeve Harrigan's (Helen Mirren) days were numbered. But it turns out Jan was the one to pay the piper, and if anyone was going to go down in the season finale, she was surely the least deserving.

Early on, "Mobland" Season 2 proved that it hadn't lost a step in comparison to the first run of episodes. It might even have outdone Season 1, thanks in large part to Johnny Flynn as villain Frankie Cooper, who has been a non-stop delight to watch as the flamboyant, psychopathic London gangster. But the show's been firing on all cylinders from the very first episode of Season 2, in which Pierce Brosnan's Conrad Harrigan dual-wielded his way through an entire gang at a race track.

Since then, we've seen the Harrigan crime family come close to collapse. A campaign of violence waged by Frankie at the behest of corrupt U.S. Ambassador Katherine "Kat" McAllister (Janet McTeer) almost wiped out the Harrigans for good. In the season finale, however, Harry Da Souza pulls off an impossibly brilliant plan to finally oust Kat and capture Frankie, all while restoring his criminal employers to their former glory. But there's an unsettling aspect to the whole thing. By the end of the episode, nobody has died, leaving you with a sense that something truly terrible is about to happen.

The final scene sees Harry pull up to Conrad's home in the Cotswolds, leaving Jan and Gina Da Souza in the car. While Harry's inside, Gina and Jan leave the car for a chat. Meanwhile, Eddie Harrigan plants Semtex under the passenger seat and is just about to hit the detonate button when he receives a call from Colin Morgan's Kelly "Mad Dog" O'Connor. Startled, he drops the detonator just as poor old Jan gets back in the car. Boom. Harry and Gina watch the brutal scene unfold before their eyes. Eddie is surely a dead man.

Jan Da Souza's only real crime (apart from shooting Alex Fine's Donnie) has been sticking around while Harry Da Souza and his criminal cohorts engage in ever more dangerous conduct. Otherwise, she's about as innocent as a "MobLand" character can be.

Now, with "MobLand" Season 3 already in production, the question becomes, what sort of fallout will we see from this shocking turn of events? Surely, Eddie isn't making it out alive. The walls are already closing in on the Harrigan scion, and this cockup seals the deal.

Episode 5 of "MobLand" Season 2 showcased the dark side of a "Star Trek" legend when Colm Meaney portrayed an Irish gangster by the name of Medusa. Eddie was sent to kill Medusa but ultimately failed to carry out the hit, forcing Harry to finish the job. Now, Medusa's son, Mad Dog, is out for revenge. But with Eddie now having killed Jan, he'll surely face Harry's wrath, too. Can he really survive the vengeful rage of both Harry and Mad Dog?

Meanwhile, there's Gina Da Souza, who has been teetering on the verge of embracing her father's criminal life all season. Jan's death will either push her away for good or prove to be her villain origin story. It might make for a decent storyline if Harry follows through on his promise to mentor Gina and turn her into a criminal force to be reckoned with. For now, we'll have to wait to see how things play out, but it's truly exciting to see "MobLand" continuing to be the best show it can be.

Shadowheart is getting her own origin story, with a new mystery set before the events of the hit RPG

The world of Baldur’s Gate 3 is expanding beyond video games once again, with a new official prequel novel set to explore the darker corners of the Forgotten Realms. The upcoming book will take readers beneath the streets of Baldur’s Gate, where a murder threatens to expose the secrets of a secretive religious order.

Titled Baldur’s Gate 3: Shadowheart, the upcoming fantasy novel comes from Tasha Suri, the World Fantasy Award-winning author of the Burning Kingdoms trilogy. It is scheduled to arrive on June 8, 2027, and is available to preorder now at major retailers.

As the title suggests, the story centers on Shadowheart, the cleric of Shar who became one of the most popular companions in Larian Studios' hit RPG.

According to the official book description, Shadowheart is a devoted follower of the goddess of darkness and loss. Living beneath Baldur’s Gate in a secretive underground church, she has embraced the belief that sacrificing memories is the key to gaining strength.

However, when a member of her religious order is murdered in the city's wealthy Upper City, Shadowheart is tasked with investigating alongside several fellow acolytes. Among them are an ambitious Griefguard named Mirie, a cynical propagandist named Caldan, and Nocturne, a charming quartermaster whose intentions Shadowheart has reason to question.The investigation soon reveals that Baldur’s Gate's wealthiest district has plenty of secrets of its own. As Shadowheart encounters unfamiliar temptations and begins questioning the comforts of her faith, she must solve the murder before her devotion is called into question.

The novel offers another opportunity to explore the backstories and world of Baldur’s Gate 3 beyond the game itself. While the book's description doesn't reveal exactly how its events connect to the RPG's broader timeline, its focus on Shadowheart's life within Shar's church should give fans a closer look at the character's history.

The Shadowheart novel is the latest expansion of the Baldur’s Gate 3 universe beyond video games. Astarion, another fan-favorite companion, has already received his own prequel novel written by T. Kingfisher, alongside other character-focused stories and comics. The franchise is also heading to television, with HBO developing an official Baldur’s Gate series from The Last of Us co-creator Craig Mazin. Unlike the upcoming Shadowheart novel, the show is expected to pick up after the events of Baldur’s Gate 3.

Baldur’s Gate 3: Shadowheart launches June 8, 2027.

#3594. Why The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping Is The Darkest Movie In The Series

The following post contains spoilers for "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping."

It's rare for a franchise to get better after 4 or 5 movies, especially when they are prequels that explore questions no one needed answered. It didn't work for "Star Wars," it didn't work for "Harry Potter," and it shouldn't work for "Hunger Games." At best, these prequels just introduced characters that don't matter in the large scheme of things because everything they do or accomplish gets erased in the original story, at worst they try so hard to answer questions no one cares about that it ends up tarnishing the original work.

And yet, when it comes to "Hunger Games," not only has the franchise improved with time, but the two spin-off prequels are arguably better than even the original series. The latest film, "Sunrise on the Reaping" deepens what came before, while introducing new characters that are as engaging as those we know and add to the larger worldbuilding of Panem. Or, as /Film's review puts it, "Beyond the shock value, this story remains human, emotional, and gripping from beginning to end."

Even if this movie doesn't have the compelling romance that was central to "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes," it delivers a harrowing tale of rebellion. What's more, this is somehow the darkest movie in the "Hunger Games" series, and it's not even close. Not just in terms of deaths — though there are some truly brutal deaths in the movie (which are somehow tamer than the book!) — but also in the overall tone the movie explores. This is the "Hunger Games" equivalent of "Andor" or "Rogue One," a bleak tragedy about one man who dared stand up against a tyrannical government and paid for it with everything he had.

The "Hunger Games" movies are full of death and suffering; it's part of the game. But "Sunrise on the Reaping" takes it to another level. Though it takes a long while before the nearly 3-hour runtime gets to the actual games, there's a feeling of hopelessness from the first moment. Early on, a kid gets shot for trying to escape the Reaping. Later, on the day of the opening ceremony, the youngest tribute from District 12, Loella, gets brutally killed in a chariot accident.

But it's not just the fact that there are plenty of deaths, or that they're horrible to watch. Sure, seeing poor Ampert get completely mauled by a swarm of cute forest animals and Maysilee Donner getting gored to death by birds is harrowing. The Capitol doesn't just kill children; it tortures them and pulls them apart and makes their parents watch.

Indeed, more than the deaths themselves, it's the meanness around them that makes this movie stand out. When Loella dies, it isn't a murder done by another tribute trying to get an advantage. Instead, it's an accident caused by Capitol audiences throwing flares at the parade circuit knowing full well it will cause the chariot horses to go berserk, because they want to see the tributes suffer. Compared to every other "Hunger Games" movie, the tributes are not only livestock sent to slaughter, or pawns in a political game. Here, they are subjects of absolute torture, playthings to be slowly toyed with and brutalized before getting discarded for the pleasure of others.

We especially see this in the presence of Ampert, whom we learn is only in the games as a punishment for his father Beetee's rebellious activities. Beetee is forced to mentor his own son and then watch him die.

Throughout "Sunrise on the Reaping," there is a sense of hopelessness and inevitability. We know that, eventually, the Hunger Games end and the Capitol falls — but the characters in the movie don't know that. At every turn, Haymitch and his allies see their every effort get squashed and mocked. Their attempts at leveling the playfield just a little bit are met with overwhelming force. Even before the games begin, Haymitch knows he'll never get to go back home because President Snow has personally seen to it that Haymitch dies for his insubordination during the opening ceremony.

Then we get to the third act, where the movie just becomes a cruel feel-bad experience, as Plutarch Heavensbee convinces Snow to let Haymitch survive to prolong his suffering. Haymitch is forced to watch Maysilee die brutally at the hands of waterbird mutts while he is virtually unscathed. Then, even after he wins the games, Haymitch discovers that the televised games were heavily edited to make him look selfish and cowardly, a traitor to every one of his allies, who won only because he was lucky. As if that wasn't enough, Haymitch has to see his family and his girlfriend die horrible deaths after he goes back home from the death games, in what's without a doubt the most nihilistic ending in the franchise.

It makes sense, however. "Sunrise on the Reaping" takes place at a pivotal moment in the "Hunger Games" timeline, at the height of President Snow's power. We are far removed from the games being almost canceled due to lack of interest like in the previous movie, but also far removed from the simmering rebellion of the original movies. Here, Snow gets away with everything, and he relishes in the cruelty of his games.

#3593. Zelda Meets Baldur's Gate 3 In Pirate RPG That's Free To Download Until November 26

Imagine taking the exploration and secrets of The Legend of Zelda, blending in the branching quests and consequential decisions of Baldur’s Gate 3, and dropping the whole thing onto a cursed pirate island. Sounds like an unusual combination, but one indie RPG brings these elements together, with dangerous creatures, challenging boss fights and multiple endings. Better yet, PC players can claim it for free for a limited time.

Mark of the Deep, developed by Mad Mimic and released in January 2025, is now available on the Epic Games Store for free. The game follows Marcus “Rookie” Ramsey, whose ship is wrecked on an island that most people know only through rumors. With the rest of his crew, the Angry Mermaids, missing, Rookie must explore the island and uncover the mystery behind its curse, which is tied to its native inhabitants, known as the Old Folks.

You see Zelda here once you look closely at how the island unfolds. Mark of the Deep uses an isometric, top-down view and encourages players to explore its connected areas. Rookie gradually gains new abilities that change how he moves through the world and handles enemies. Some routes stay out of reach until he has the right skill, giving players a reason to return to explored places. There are also secrets and side quests to find along the way.

This isn’t a party-based, turn-based RPG, though, so the Baldur’s Gate comparison isn’t about the genre. Mark of the Deep is a single-player action adventure, and its fights take more from the Soulslike genre. Its role-playing side comes through in the people Rookie meets, the quests he can take on and the decisions he makes. The game lets players help characters affected by the island’s corruption, and those choices can influence how the story ends.

For the crucial part of combat, the developers list more than 80 enemies and 16 bosses, including abyssal creatures, undead enemies and cultists. Rookie can unlock new skills, weapons and trinkets as he progresses, allowing him to improve his fighting options. Boss encounters can be challenging, requiring players to learn enemy attack patterns and adjust their approach.

The island also has plenty to explore, although the lack of an in-game map can make navigation frustrating at times. Its atmosphere and exploration are appealing, but players should be prepared to spend some time figuring out where to go next.

There’s a time limit on the giveaway, but not on playing the game once it has been claimed. Search for Mark of the Deep on the Epic Games Store and add it to your library before the offer ends on November 26 at 4 p.m. UTC. You don’t need to download and install the game to claim it for free; just add it and a copy becomes yours forever.

Mark of the Deep is also a fairly modest download by current PC standards: you don’t need a powerful rig to play this Zelda-inspired pirate adventure. For your reference, Epic lists a 5GB storage requirement, 4GB RAM and a dual-core 2.4GHz processor as the minimum specifications.

The Legend of Zelda franchise follows the adventures of Link, an elf-like Hylian, and Princess Zelda as they protect the land of Hyrule from the evil warlord-turned-demon king Ganon. The series is known for its mix of action, adventure, and puzzle-solving elements, often revolving around the collection of the Triforce, a powerful relic left by the goddesses who created Hyrule.

#3592. These Are the Best Ways to Encrypt Your Email

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

As this in-depth explainer from Adaptive Security describes, most emails are encrypted in transit via Transport Layer Security (TLS), which prevents anyone from reading your message as it travels from server to server. However, encryption is temporarily stripped at each server: content is received and processed in plaintext and then re-encrypted when it leaves, meaning it could be read, logged, and distributed by the server provider.

Emails are also typically encrypted at rest—for example, while sitting on Google's servers and in a Gmail recipient's inbox. But this only prevents someone with physical access to the server hardware from reading messages, as Google still holds the encryption key and can access stored data. And, as PCMag points out, Google is scanning your messages to a degree, and it (along with other email providers) can and will hand emails over to law enforcement and government agencies in some cases.

If you have an account with a major email provider like Gmail, Outlook, or Apple Mail, you can add a third-party tool that layers an encryption protocol like OpenPGP on top of your existing account. PCMag recommends PreVeil, SecureMyEmail, and Virtru (which is limited to Gmail users in Chrome) for those who want to keep their current emails. Mailvelope is a browser add-on (and therefore a desktop-only tool) available in Chrome, Firefox, and Edge, though it can also be installed on other browsers, like Brave, that are built on the same architecture. FlowCrypt integrates with Gmail and Google Workspace on desktop and mobile.

Note that enterprise users of Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 have access to true end-to-end encryption without third-party add-ons. Gmail's Confidential mode and Outlook's Encrypt feature, available to all users, are not E2EE equivalents, as Google and Microsoft, respectively, still manage the keys.

For those who are willing to start fresh with a new email address (or who have a custom domain), providers like Proton Mail or Tuta offer native end-to-end encryption. The caveat: by default, this is only between users on the same service, so from one Proton user to another. If you want to send an end-to-end encrypted email from Proton to a Gmail user, for example, you have to set up password protection (and share the password via another secure channel) or use a PGP-compatible tool like those listed above. You can also Proton's Gmail integration does allow for end-to-end encryption, but only if both Gmail parties are using the Proton integration.

#3591. 5 Best New Movies And Shows To Stream This Weekend On Netflix, HBO Max, Paramount Plus, And More (Nov. 20-22)

It's almost Thanksgiving, and as you prepare to fly home (well, depending on if planes are allowed in the sky when you need to do that), you might be feeling a weird sense of dread about sleeping in your parent's house next to their dusty Peloton on your old Spider-Man sheets. Why not binge-watch some stuff to deal with those feelings?

I've got you covered. There's a handful of new releases coming to major streaming platforms this week, and honestly? This is a pretty good handful. While major titles like "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" captivate people who decide to head to a movie theater and hang out there for a few hours, maybe you're looking for a scenario where you don't have to wear real pants and can pause whatever you're watching whenever the fancy strikes you. From one of the biggest horror hits in recent memory to the final season of a mystery box series to an offbeat biopic helmed by a Canadian comedy favorite, here are five movies or shows to stream on Netflix, Disney+, Paramount+, Peacock, or HBO Max over November 20-22, 2026.

Besides the creepypasta horror hit "Backrooms," "Obsession" is the other film credited with keeping the horror genre young and fresh in 2026 — and it's not just because Kane Parsons and Curry Barker, the respective directors of those films, were born in 2005 and 1999. (As someone born in 1990, I admittedly do think about that a lot.) "Obsession," which is now available to watch on Netflix, and was completely devised by Barker, tells the story of Baron "Bear" Bailey (Michael Johnston), a young man carrying a torch for his platonic friend Nikki Freeman (Inde Navarrette, who may just end up earning an Oscar nod in 2027). After using a weird artifact called the One Wish Willow that he finds at an oddities store trying to get Nikki a gift, Bear wishes that Nikki would love him more than anything in the world ... and boy, does he get his wish.

Not only does Nikki really love Bear after the One Wish Willow takes effect, she seems unable to leave his side or focus on anything else — as if she's under some sort of hypnotic spell. "Obsession" is a dark, unsettling, and tightly directed horror film that interrogates Nikki's agency, Bear's distinct role in his own downfall, and what happens when you want someone to love you without actually knowing how they feel in the first place. "Obsession" is innovative, compelling, and one of the most popular movies in recent memory — and now, it's on Netflix.

When we last saw the titular Yellowjackets — a teenage soccer team stranded in the Canadian wilderness after a plane crash nearly two years prior — during the Showtime series' penultimate season in 2025, the teenagers in that wilderness were on the precipice of being rescued in the late 1990s. Meanwhile, in the more modern timeline, their adult counterparts are still trying to cover up whatever happened out in those woods. Now, in the fourth and final season (which earned a solid review right here at /Film), there are three timelines: one where the teenagers finish out their time in the wilderness, one after they've been rescued and dropped back into their "normal" lives in New Jersey, and that adult one, where all hell threatens to break loose as Shauna Shipman (Melanie Lynskey) continues to break bad after absolutely losing her s**t in Season 3.

Jasmin Savoy Brown, Liv Hewson, Sophie Thatcher, Sammi Hanratty, Courtney Eaton, and Sophie Nélisse make up the core of the teenage cast, while in the adult one, the always wonderful Lynskey is joined by Tawny Cypress, Christina Ricci, and even Oscar winner Hilary Swank (after former adult actors Lauren Ambrose, Juliette Lewis, and Simone Kessell exited at various points, though it's easy to imagine that they could reappear in Season 4 flashbacks at some point). As someone who's been watching this puzzle box show since the very beginning, I'll admit I have substantive doubts about "Yellowjackets" landing the plane (and it's not like its track record with these things is pretty great, if you consider the pun), but I'll definitely be watching Season 4 following its premiere on Paramount+ with Showtime on November 20, with new episodes airing weekly.

To call "Tony" a biopic feels ... sort of misleading. Directed by Matt Johnson (who recently wowed comedy nerds, a term I use affectionately, with "Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie" and cut his teeth on another biopic of sorts, "Blackberry"), the film follows a young Anthony Bourdain, played by the wry, excellent Dominic Sessa, as he learns a thing or two about life and proper oyster-shucking technique during a fateful summer in Providence, Rhode Island. Alongside a chef who never gets a proper name (Antonio Banderas) and who owns a small seafood place called "The Flagship," the titular Tony, who keeps insisting he's not an aspiring culinary expert but a writer with a fellowship (not true), pursues the girl of his dreams — photographer Nancy (Emilia Jones) — and gets into trouble with his fellow chef Sal (Leo Woodall) as he tries to figure out who he is and what he wants out of this experience.

I didn't love "Tony" as much as many of my peers (see: /Film's own Bill Bria's review of the movie), but if you mentally remove the Bourdain of it all from the film and enjoy it as a showcase for Sessa's talents and Johnson's comedic timing, you'll probably get way more mileage out of this fresh, generally fun film. "Tony" is on HBO Max now, which makes sense, as its studio, A24, tends to premiere its movies there when they come to streaming.

Author Rick Riordan co-created the Disney+ series "Percy Jackson and the Olympians" for Disney+ along with Jonathan E. Steinberg ("Jericho"), and whether you're a fan of Riordan's original books, enjoyed the short-lived "Percy Jackson" film franchise, or have been waiting for this show to return since Season 2 concluded back in January of 2026, you'll be happy to hear that Season 3 premiered on Disney+ on November 20. In the inaugural season released in late 2023, the action follows the plot of Riordan's novel "The Lightning Thief" and sees the titular Percy, played by Walker Scobell, discovering that not only are Greek gods real, he has magical powers and can learn how to wield them at a place called Camp Half-Blood. After using the Empire State Building to reach Olympus at the end of Season 1, Season 2 catches up with Percy during the events of Riordan's book "The Sea of Monsters," which brings a bunch of elements of "The Odyssey" into play.

So, what about Season 3? It's set to follow Riordan's third novel, "The Titan's Curse," where Percy has to face off against Kronos and his army to rescue the goddess Artemis (Dafne Keen) and his friend Annabeth (Leah Sava Jeffries). The first two episodes of Season 3 dropped on Disney+ on November 20, with two episodes debuting every Friday throughout its run.

"Alien: Romulus" came out in 2024, and now, it's available to stream on Peacock. Fede Álvarez's entry into the storied "Alien" franchise features tons of rising stars like Cailee Spaeny, David Jonsson (who's gearing up to play the son of the late "Black Panther" star Chadwick Boseman's T'Challa in the Marvel Cinematic Universe), Spike Fearn, and Isabela Merced, and as it unfolds, we see half a dozen young colonists trying to navigate the deep recesses of space and finding dangerous creatures inside of an old space station. As orphan Marie Raines "Rain" Carradine (Spaeny) gathers the crew, including her adopted android brother Andy (Jonsson), her ex-boyfriend Tyler (Archie Renaux), his pregnant sister Kay (Merced), their cousin Bjorn (Fearn), and his adoptive sister Navarro (Aileen Wu), they encounter enemies left and right, leaving them shaken and fighting for their lives as they try to reach safety.

#3590. 10 Privacy Hacks Every Mac User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Enabling the macOS Firewall (which is off by default) adds a layer of protection against external devices on your wifi network, as well as unauthorized apps from initiating a connection to your device. Turning on Stealth Mode prevents your Mac from even responding to these requests, essentially making it invisible to anything that's scanning a network you're connected to. This makes it more difficult for hackers and malware to know your device exists, much less attack it. This can interfere with certain essential activity when you're on your home network, but it's a valuable security setting when on public wifi. You can leave Firewall on all the time and enable Stealth Mode only as needed. Go to Settings > Network > Firewall, flip the toggle, then hit Options to manage Stealth Mode.

Images and screenshots contain metadata, such as timestamps, device and hardware details, and, in the case of photos, physical location. Much of this information is stripped automatically when you share files to social media or via encrypted messaging apps, but if you're sending them via text or email, posting to forums, or sharing over AirDrop, metadata remains intact. You can easily remove metadata from your images right on your desktop. Select the file and hit control + click to bring up an options menu, then go to Quick Actions > Convert Image. Uncheck the box next to Preserve Metadata, then hit Convert. (This is also useful for quickly converting HEIC to JPEG without opening a separate app.)

If you're using iCloud to store photos, files, and device backups, your data is encrypted on Apple's servers and in transit. Apple still holds the decryption key, which is useful if you somehow get locked out of your account and need help recovering it, but for sensitive data—including device backups—end-to-end encryption is the most secure way to ensure no one but you can gain access. Advanced Data Protection is an opt-in setting for iCloud that encrypts your information end to end. You'll need to set up an alternative recovery method, such as your device passcode with two-factor authentication, a recovery contact, or a recovery key. Be careful, though: If you lose access to this recovery method, you will lose your data. You can enable Advanced Data Protection on your Mac under System Settings > [Your Name] > iCloud > Advanced Data Protection > Turn On. Note that some iCloud data, including passwords and payment methods, are already end-to-end encrypted by default.

#3587. Is A24 Finally Big Enough to Be Considered a Major Studio?

Earlier this year when IndieWire reported that A24 had settled a dispute with Marcus Theaters over theatrical terms, a back and forth that kept some of A24‘s summer titles like “The Invite,” “Tony,” and “Onslaught” out of the fourth-largest chain in the country, the reason was because of a debate over A24’s size. When you have blockbusters as big as “Backrooms” and “Marty Supreme,” why would you still want theatrical terms that lump you in with the specialized, little guys?

This is the question that Hollywood — and even perhaps A24 internally — should start asking: Should A24 now be considered a major studio? Should A24 be in the same conversation as Disney, Universal, Sony, Paramount, Warner Bros., Netflix, Amazon MGM, Apple, and Lionsgate? Related Stories Bill Hader’s Feature Directorial Debut ‘They Know’ Lands at Black Bear Why Good Voice Acting Doesn’t Have to Happen in Isolation

In some regards, this is a semantic discussion. Whether A24 is in that made-up tier of six to nine corporate conglomerates that the trades call “majors” doesn’t mean a lick to the general public. Audiences know they care about the A24 brand and logo in the same way they pay attention to the brands of Marvel, Pixar, Blumhouse, IMAX, and a select few others making movies today, and the rest is mostly gravy. Postrak found that on average, 70 percent of people who see A24 movies on opening weekend go to theaters more often than others, at least monthly, so the brand has an impact. But whether it has theatrical terms on par with Paramount or with Bleecker Street doesn’t matter in the slightest.

In another sense, whether A24 is a major studio and not some cool upstart indie with a lot of scale matters a whole lot. It matters to investors, it matters to people who care about the A24 brand, it matters to theater owners, and it should matter to A24 itself as it defines what it wants to be moving forward. Netflix wasn’t always considered a major, legacy studio, but their size and success got so undeniable that you had to put them in the same conversation as the other majors who drove trends, who influenced deal making for stars and creators, and who eventually had to reach the same labor terms as everyone else.

A24 might soon be in the same boat, if it isn’t already. Led by the success of “Backrooms,” the company has entered a new echelon in 2026, one that has allowed it to rival studios that were once much larger than A24 in every facet. Now those lines have blurred, A24’s budgets and the grosses those films are able to generate have grown, it’s earning sizable $75 million investments from places like Google and is in the mix to buy properties like Letterboxd, arguably more than others have speculated its time to sell.

Answering whether A24 is a “major” isn’t a simple question with one answer. There’s several criteria we could look at to make a case in either direction.

A24 through November 15 in 2026 has earned $526.6 million at the domestic box office, according to data from Rentrak. It was led by “Backrooms,” which made $197 million domestic, but that’s not even half its overall haul. This year, that’s roughly $175 million above the next-highest specialized distributor in Focus Features ($351.8 million), which released the even more successful “Obsession” ($263.4 million) this year, and it’s well above the likes of other indie rivals like Neon, Fathom, GKIDS, Angel Studios, Black Bear, and Searchlight.

It has also more than doubled what it brought in across a full year in 2025, a 124 percent increase so far (it still has its big awards play “The Debut” opening in December and “Club Kid” going wider), and it’s nearly four times where it was in 2023 when A24’s total domestic box office was $136.7 million and its biggest release of the year was “Talk to Me,” which made $44.2 million domestic. Four of A24’s movies this year (“Backrooms,” “You Can See Everything,” “The Drama,” and “Primetime”) surpassed that figure.

It’s safe to say it puts A24 in a tier of its own above the other indies. But does it rise to the level of a major? As recently as last year, the answer was squarely no. But A24 in 2026, per Rentrak, commands a 6.0 percent market share on the year so far. That puts it fifth on the year so far, ahead of Warner Bros., Paramount, and Lionsgate (those numbers will change as some other tentpoles emerge). It would not have even cracked the top 10 last year when its market share was just 2.7 percent and was largely driven by the late-year success of “Marty Supreme.”

A24 doesn’t have and probably won’t for some time field a movie that can realistically sniff $1 billion worldwide the way many major studios manage to pump out each and every year. But receipts don’t lie, and what makes this realistically sustainable for A24 to repeat year after year is how much it has grown.

A24 is releasing in the vicinity of 16 to 18 movies annually, and that puts it easily on par with legacy studios like Disney, Sony, Warner Bros., and Paramount. Skydance, which now owns Paramount and WB, will release 30+ movies a year, but between the two studios. Universal tends to get into the 20s, but only when you combine its output with that of Focus. Netflix puts out way, way more than the whole bunch, but they’re naturally streaming movies that include low-budget genre movies and documentaries.

Some of A24’s films each year are still acquisitions out of festivals, which was the case this year with both “The Invite” (Sundance) and “Club Kid” (Cannes). But like the other majors, A24 produces and finances a large majority of its movies independently, with a handful of co-productions. Importantly, it works with new filmmakers and forges relationships so that they stay in their pipeline, whether they’re newcomers like Lance Oppenheim and Kane Parsons or veterans like Celine Song, Alex Garland, and Ari Aster who have returned to A24 time and again.

A24’s international distribution has it partnering with other overseas distributors, which is structurally different from major studios that have robust international distribution arms, but it has still released some of its movies in English-language territories like the UK. You can imagine that as A24 continues to grow, that could be one area of natural expansion.

Where A24 still lags significantly behind other majors though is in its overall content spend, a number that A24 doesn’t publicly disclose. Netflix had a content spend this year of about $20 billion. Disney was around $24 billion and recently projected to increase to $26 billion in its next fiscal year. Maybe if A24 starts picking up sports rights to the NBA it can start getting into that ballpark.

But even when focusing just on film, something like “Backrooms” was still produced for a modest $10 million, whereas other studios have multiple titles that well exceed $100 million in production budget alone. We do know though that its budgets have increased dramatically as A24 pursues more tentpole properties. “Marty Supreme” was previously its most expensive title, but its adaptation of the video game “Elden Ring” will blow that out of the water, with a budget in the vicinity of $170 million or above. That kind of investment carries risks. There are Marvel movies that don’t cost that much.

A24 hasn’t yet put its stamp on a four-quadrant, animated Dr. Seuss movie or something similar that would easily make you think it has ambitions of becoming a major studio, but the types of movies it has released has grown more varied over the years. It has horror movies, adult comedies, biopics, thrillers, and even, of course, documentaries like “You Can See Everything,” an area that it looked like A24 was scaling back on not too long ago. When “Elden Ring” opens it will squarely be an action fantasy, and the studio has other genre films, comedies, thrillers, and more in the works for next year.

You can also see A24’s diversity in how it’s approaching awards plays versus commercial titles or specialized fare. Something like “The Drama” this year opened wide right out of the gate given its star power, whereas others like “The Invite” and “Tony” have stuck to platform releases before going wider. And those smaller, art house titles alongside its genre movies and its tentpoles are still a key part of its business model and identity. Movies like “Pillion,” “Mother Mary,” and “The Moment” have done business on a much smaller scale, but are still key in helping the company get to that 6 percent share (they lost money on some, though).

The definition of major studio today has evolved to the point that the movie division is just a component of a massive media conglomerate, one that also includes television, streaming, gaming, sports, news, theme parks, and other ancillary businesses. If you’re Apple or Amazon, your movie studio is a small cog, practically a loss leader, in the larger tech empire. It gives these companies valuations of tens of billions of dollars, and it’s why A24 could still be a target for M&A if it chooses to sell.

A24 does have its own record label for music and original movie score releases and vinyl pressing, it has been producing a podcast since 2018, it owns the Cherry Lane Theater in New York for stage productions and concerts, it sells plenty of kooky merchandise, and it even has a membership program and campus ambassador program that have seen growth in recent years. They’re all things that suggest the company has more on its mind than movies.

And as we wrote earlier this week, its TV unit has quietly had as strong a year as its film team. A24 has spread series across virtually every major streaming service, all of them again varying in genre, pedigree, and budget. It’s not just the number of shows that has expanded but the executive team to support them.

It may be a strength that A24 doesn’t have its own SVOD service to support all these shows and movies, or a broadcast network or cable channel that could further complicate things. Those businesses are very costly to operate and some are in the decline phase of their trajectories. Yet, it inherently keeps A24 in a lower tier compared to other major studios that do have their own distribution apparatus for television and can license content from other studios like A24. While Gen Z might get excited about the idea of an A24 streaming service, that’s an area of growth that’s less likely to occur in the short term. Well, unless A24 wants to raise a lot more capital.

This is the qualitative assessment of whether A24 should be considered a “major” studio, the one that doesn’t lean on numbers and instead just goes on feel. A24 might argue that it is one of one, that it doesn’t belong to the world of major studios, and that the baggage that comes with that status isn’t worth it. But its leaders probably believe A24 is a step above the other indies that are almost solely distributors. Do we really think the same company that is taking a chance on movies as weird as “You Can See Everything” or “Primetime” is equivalent to a studio that might make the odd “Digger,” but is mostly interested in producing “A Minecraft Movie” and “Superman?” Is it fair to lump in A24 with Focus, Searchlight, and Sony Pictures Classics, which are quite literally just specialized labels within larger studios?

All that could be true, but it doesn’t mean we shouldn’t reassess how we view A24 as a company or how we handicap its hits and misses in the same way we would with Disney or Netflix. Even if we’re not ready to call A24 a “major,” there’s certainly a major shift in where A24 sits in this industry. With great success comes an even greater spotlight.

#3586. If Your Google Pixel's Camera Is Suddenly Broken, Here's the Fix

Updates are generally good for your devices. The latest Chrome update, for example, patches an actively exploited security vulnerability, while Apple's latest updates stop people from seeing iMessages they shouldn't have access to. In most cases, it's beneficial to update your tech to the latest software version whenever possible.

Sadly, updates aren't all perfect, as Google Pixel users are discovering this week. As reported by Android Authority, Google's November update apparently shipped with a bug that breaks some Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 cameras. Seeing as Pixels are rather famous for their shooters, this is a decidedly unfortunate glitch.

Here's the situation: Following the November update, some users are opening their Pixel Camera apps to find an error that reads, "Something went wrong. Close and open the Camera app again," with a "Learn More" link to, well, learn more. Others aren't receiving the error, but are instead running into a blank Camera viewfinder, as if the lens is totally covered. What's more, some users are reportedly saying that the issue is present on third-party camera apps, not just the Pixel Camera app. That would imply this is an issue with the camera system-wide, not just the Pixel Camera app itself.

To be clear, it doesn't seem like this is a universal issue. It's not like all Pixel users are now running with broken cameras. But based on the forum complaints Android Authority discovered, it seems reasonable to assume that this glitch isn't limited to just a handful of unlucky Pixel owners.

Luckily, there is an apparent workaround here, though it's not totally obvious. Some users are having no luck restarting their Pixels, while others report that a factory reset wasn't enough to restore camera functionality.

What does appear to work, however, is shutting your Pixel down and waiting five minutes or so. It's not clear why, but giving your Pixel a chance to "breathe" seems to shake the glitch and bring back your camera. As Android Authority reports, that fix comes from "Diamond and Gold product experts" on Google's Support forum.

If your Pixel's camera is giving you grief following the November update, this workaround is definitely worth a try—especially since more drastic measures don't actually seem to do anything. As the issue does seem to be rather widespread, I wouldn't be surprised to see Google issue a patch in the coming days. But until then, turning your phone off for five minutes may be a decent compromise.
