#3585. All 14 Witches In Agatha All Along Explained

Warning: This article contains SPOILERS for Agatha All Along

Agatha All Along's central witch coven comprises seven different characters, each with their own specialties, powers, stories, and Marvel connections. Agatha All Along's MCU story stems from the climactic ending of WandaVision. The latter show centered on the Scarlet Witch and her inadvertent enslavement of the town of Westview. The villain of the show was Agatha herself, played by Kathryn Hahn once more in Agatha All Along's cast of characters.

Given that WandaVision is one of the better-ranked MCU shows thus far, Agatha All Along was highly anticipated, especially considering the former show's creator and writer, Jac Schaeffer, possesses the same roles in the latter. What makes Agatha All Along's MCU story even more interesting, however, is the show's new batch of characters.

The series is a fun, spooky, Halloween-inspired MCU show centering on witches from across the MCU, meaning each character has their own intriguing stories, power sets, connections to Agatha, and links to Marvel Comics.

Beginning with the titular character, Agatha Harkness is a former witch from Salem, Massachusetts. Agatha belonged to her own coven long ago but was accused of practicing dark magic during the Salem witch trials. After her coven attempted to cast her out, Agatha's dark magic attacked her peers, including her mother, killing them and setting Agatha down a path of villainy and evil. 300 years later, Agatha was drawn to Westview after Wanda Maximoff covered the town in a witch hex, with the former seeking to harness the latter's chaos magic.

Agatha failed to draw Wanda's power from her and had her own drained in the process, leading the latter to enslave the former in Westview seemingly permanently. In Agatha All Along, the titular witch is freed from her prison and embarks on a quest down the Witches Road. At the end of it, Agatha hopes to recover what will make her whole again: her powers.

In the comics, Agatha's origins are similar to those from WandaVision. Agatha was involved in the Salem Witch Trials in the comics, only with the difference that she orchestrated them to cull the weak from her coven. Over the centuries, Agatha spends a lot of time trying to build her power in multiple covens, training several magic users, and even fighting in wars like the American Revolutionary War and defeating Nazi sorcerers during World War II.

Eventually, Agatha crossed paths with The Fantastic Four when she became the governess of Franklin Richards, often aiding the team and even teaching Franklin to hone his powers. Through The Fantastic Four, she met Wanda Maximoff. Agatha became the mentor to Wanda and other magic users in the modern Marvel Comics era and has been killed and subsequently resurrected multiple times. In the current continuity, Agatha is alive, though is rarely seen in stories.

Like the other strong sorcerers of the Marvel universe, Agatha's powers are a gateway to almost endless abilities. From energy and elemental manipulation and binding spells to dimensional manipulation, flight, force fields, and illusions, Agatha is one of the most powerful magic users in the Marvel Comics pantheon. This is without mentioning her telepathy, telekinesis, and the tens of other abilities she possesses through her magical training.

While Agatha's powers are gone in Agatha All Along as a result of Wanda's spell on the witch at the end of WandaVision, it appears Harkness still believes she has the ability to absorb the powers of other magic-users if they direct their abilities at her. However, it's unclear whether this is indeed true, or rather the character's own hopes as she attempts everything to retrieve her former abilities once more.

One of the other witches who joins Agatha and Teen down the Witches Road is Lilia Calderu, played by Patti LuPone. In the context of Agatha’s coven, Calderu serves as an expert in divination. Divination is the practice of seeking knowledge about the future via supernatural means. In Calderu’s case in Agatha All Along, she suffers from various visions and flashes of foresight, making her seem somewhat more unhinged than the witches around her.

Because of her powers, Lilia is shown to be aware of some of the details of Agatha's past, telling the witch that she knows Agatha has been under the influence of "someone you hurt" and who then took her agency for 3 years. This - combined with Lilia's own experience of witch history, since Agatha suggests she's 450 years old - it's likely Lilia could provide more insight about Agatha's backstory as the show continues, since she's clearly able to access information that the witch may otherwise not be willing to reveal.

In the comics, Lilia Calderu is the descendant of the first Baron of Mordo. Calderu is part of a coven that is responsible for the protection of the Book of Cagliostro. Interestingly, Lilia is linked to Wanda Maximoff’s origins in Marvel Comics, with her divination powers providing visions that Wanda will become immensely powerful.

Lilia’s story ended with Karl Mordo romancing her to gain her trust. Mordo stole the Book of Cagliostro, breaking Lilia’s heart and leading her down a path of revenge. Despite enlisting the aid of Doctor Strange, Lilia was killed by a Living Gargoyle searching for Mordo.

Agatha All Along will see Alice Wu-Gulliver (Ali Ahn) join the titular character’s coven to journey down the Witches Road. Where Lilia Calderu excels in divination, Alice Wu-Gulliver is described as a protection witch. This means Wu-Gulliver is likely the strongest of the seven regarding shielding spells, and thus will be vital to countering the dangers of the Witches Road.

The character is shown to be using these skills to work in a mall store at the start of Agatha All Along before losing her job, which leads her to decide to join Agatha's coven and travel the Witch's Road, though her past in the armed forces is alluded to as well, suggesting there's much more to be uncovered about Wu-Gulliver. This concept is further hinted at by allusions to Alice Wu-Gulliver's mother, Lorna Wu, who is described as a witch and famous musician, and who appears to have gone mysteriously missing, possibly in the Witch's Road itself.

Ali Ahn described Alice as someone who is looking to access a magical power that has lain dormant for a while. As such, it's possible that her protection abilities will take some time to come to their full extent over the course of the show - which may leave the coven in a precarious position until that time.

In Marvel Comics, this character is born Alice Gulliver. Alice is the daughter of August Wu, the magical protector of Hong Kong, and the detective Adam Gulliver. Alice desired to become a member of the police force like her father as a teen, around the same time her mother was killed by a demonic figure. After this tragedy, Alice found that her hair had changed color from brown to the red of her mother’s. To compound this sadness, Alice’s father was later killed by one of the Chinese Triads.

Eventually, Alice became a police detective like her father, while using the inherited magical powers from her mother to her advantage. Alice started using a shortened version of her mother’s title, “The Wu,” and even teamed up with the Scarlet Witch to defeat the evil wizard Dark Tongji. The title of “The Wu” is being incorporated into Agatha All Along’s version of the character, who is named Alice Wu-Gulliver.

Agatha All Along will include the Marvel Comics character of Jennifer Kale. In Agatha All Along, Jennifer Kale is a potions witch of Agatha's newfound coven, with her skills primarily being found in alchemy and chemistry. Kale is revealed to have had her powers bound, and to be using her knowledge to make a health and beauty business wherein she creates skincare products and probiotic candles, though it's also revealed that she's dealing with an impending legal lawsuit for some of these products, suggesting things aren't going entirely smoothly.

Jennifer has been described by actor Sasheer Zamata as very sarcastic, possessing a love-hate relationship with Agatha herself. Agatha All Along plays on this, implying the pair have a notable history together that is as of yet unexplored.

In Marvel Comics, Jennifer Kale was the daughter of Joshua Kale, leader of the Cult of Zhered-Na. Zhered-Na was a powerful sorceress, with the cult existing in the Florida Everglades where the Nexus of All Realities is housed. Eventually, Jennifer took an interest in witchcraft and began dabbling in magic.

After facing off against demons and having many adventures, resulting in the discovery of a psychic connection with a creature called the Man-Thing, Jennifer became the apprentice of a wizard called Dakimh. Jennifer’s story has led her to become an ally of Ghost Rider, X-Force, and the Midnight Sons.

More so than the previous two witches explored, Jennifer Kale's Marvel Comics powers are more defined. Kale draws magic from three sources: her personal power from training, powers gained by tapping into the magical energy of the Marvel universe, and extra-dimensional powers. These three sources offer Kale a myriad of magic powers, from magic bolts, shields, dimensional portals, and teleportation, to more psychological abilities like affecting memories and charming other people. These powers are very different from Agatha All Along's description of Kale as a witch who specializes in potions.

Aubrey Plaza's Rio Vidal is one of Agatha All Along's original characters, though there are rumors she is a gender-swapped version of Marvel Comics' Emerald Warlock. Rio is described as the warrior witch of Agatha's coven, the more badass counterpart to her peers, though it is unclear what her powers are as yet. Speculation that she is Lady Death is also one of the major aspects of her character.

Rio likely has more offensive powers than the shielding, divination, and alchemical powers of her sister witches. Her fight with Agatha early in the show only reveals her fighting powers, but these could possibly have also been enhanced by whatever magic she holds.

The show has subtly suggested Plaza's character is a green witch, since Agatha avoids recruiting an earth witch placed on her list of witches to recruit who is noted to have only a black heart. Instead, Agatha recruits Mrs. Hart - who is very clearly shown to not have powers at this time - and Rio is the only witch who'd seemingly evoke this reaction. When Mrs. Hart dies, the coven summons another green witch, and Rio shows up.

The final character to make up Agatha's coven in Agatha All Along is, surprisingly, not even a witch as far as the MCU's past stories go: Sharon Davis, a.k.a. Mrs. Hart. Debra Jo Rupp first played this character in WandaVision, with Sharon Davis being a resident of Westview who became "Mrs. Hart" when under the influence of Wanda's hex. WandaVision ended with Sharon being freed from Wanda's control, making her return in Agatha All Along that much more surprising.

In a featurette for Agatha All Along, Sharon is described as the group's green witch, but Sharon was shown as having no distinct powers in WandaVision, and indeed seems to have none in the sequel show, with Agatha tricking her into joining the group. Whether Sharon Davis will become a witch in Agatha All Along remains to be seen, but she at least provides the show with an everyman character, a connection to a past MCU project, and a seventh witch for the coven intent on traveling the Witches Road.

Evanora Harkness was the mother of Agatha Harkness. She first appeared in WandaVision during flashbacks for Agatha, where it was revealed that she was the leader of the Salemites and attempted to murder Agatha during the Salem Witch Trials, accusing Agatha of betraying her coven and practicing the darkest of magic.

She appeared again in episode 5 of Agatha All Along, possessing Agatha during one of the trials. After leaving Agatha's body, Evanora tells the rest of the witches that her "coven risked everything to kill her and you fools have willingly joined her." Evanora reveals that she should have killed Agatha the moment she was born, saying she was "born evil." When Alice casts a spell on Agatha and Evanora, she leaves, keeping what her purpose was to be there a mystery.

Like Agatha and the rest of the coven, Evanora Harkness was proficient in witchcraft, leading her own coven before being killed by Agatha. Through her magic, Evanora was able to manipulate energy to her will. After her death, Evanora Harkness was able to possess Agatha's body during an episode of Agatha All Along, but it is unclear if that is exclusive to her.

The Salem Seven made their MCU debut during the events of Agatha All Along. It is revealed that they are the children of the Salemites, the coven of witches that Agatha murdered during the Salem Witch Trials. They are seen in Agatha All Along attempting to hunt down Agatha and the rest of her coven, gaining access to the Witches' Road to do so.

Agatha spared the children after killing the Salemites, but that led to them growing hateful and resentful, eventually forming a coven to get

revenge on Agatha for the murders. With them still pursuing Agatha and her coven, The Salem Seven will presumably be featured in more episodes of Agatha All Along, trying to exact their revenge.

The Salem Seven's comic book origins vary greatly compared to their MCU counterparts. In the comics, they are Nicholas Scratch's children, who is the son of Agatha Harkness. This means that Agatha is their grandmother. This is a massive change from the MCU version being the children of the Salemites, but given that Agatha's son is dead in the universe, it makes sense for them to have a different origin. In the comics, The Salem Seven went after Agatha because Scratch believed Agatha betrayed New Salem by leaving it.

Agatha All Along’s most mysterious character throughout the first five episodes was undoubtedly Joe Locke’s Teen. Eventually, Joe Locke's character was finally confirmed to be Wiccan, after a long period of speculation. It is revealed that it was Wiccan who frees Agatha from Wanda’s Hex and convinces her to take the Witches Road to retrieve her powers.

Whether he has ulterior motives for this remains to be seen, but episode 5 saw him use his powers to overcome the members of the coven, including Agatha, showing there is definitely more to this character than he initially led on.

Wanda lost her children in WandaVision and Doctor Strange 2, meaning Billy’s reincarnation could have taken place. There is still a mystery about just how Billy returned following those projects, but Agatha All Along is primed to reveal even more about his character for the remainder of the series. The two biggest questions revolving around Billy are about who put the spell on him so that no one would hear his name and how he did return.

Given the secrecy surrounding Billy so far, it is difficult to explore his comic book connections. In the comics, Billy was reincarnated from Billy Maximoff, whom the Scarlet Witch created using her reality-altering powers and a lost soul. The devil Mephisto claimed the souls for himself before being destroyed by Wanda’s magic within them. The soul of Billy was then reincarnated into Billy Kaplan, the son of two workers in New York City.

After a difficult early life, Billy found solace in his relationship with Teddy Altman, later revealed to be Hulkling, the son of Captain Marvel. After Billy discovers magical powers, he joins Marvel's Young Avengers with Hulkling, and eventually, they encounter Tommy Shepherd. It is revealed that Billy and Tommy are the reincarnated twins of Wanda and Vision, becoming known by their superhero names, Wiccan and Speed. After this, Billy undergoes several adventures alongside his boyfriend Hulkling, his brother Speed, and his other allies in the Marvel universe.

As the son of Wanda Maximoff, Billy possesses immense magical power. Perhaps his main power is reality manipulation like his mother, with Billy able to use a lot of spells by speaking what he wishes into reality, unlike the more deliberate spells of other wizards and witches. Aside from this, Billy’s other powers include astral projection, magical binding, clairvoyance, concussive blasts, elemental manipulation, flight, healing, and teleportation. Wiccan’s magic is also a gateway to many other abilities, from augmentation and telepathy to telekinesis and transmutation, to name but a few.

In Agatha All Along, he tells Agatha that he doesn't have any real powers and is looking to traverse the Witch's Road in the hopes of gaining his own. Of course, this was a lie because he uses his powers during the reveal of who he is, and is already quite strong. Why he decided to hide his abilities from Agatha and the rest of the coven is a mystery, and leaves audiences just what his motives are in Agatha All Along.

Agatha Harkness, after the events of "WandaVision," seeks to regain her magical powers. Joining forces with unexpected allies, including the son of an old adversary, she battles new mystical threats while uncovering hidden secrets in the magical realm.

#3584. Five Hacks Every Apple Watch Series 12 User Should Know

The latest Apple Watches have a lot of new features that older watches don't, so I figured it was time for a new list of hacks. While our general Apple Watch and fitness tracking hacks are still golden, Series 12 devices offer new features like native step counting, a Readiness app, an upgraded heart rate sensor, an AI-based version of Siri, and "audio intelligence" that can replay and summarize real-life conversations, within limits. Here's how to get the most out of them.

The Series 12 can finally count steps natively, a task that for some reason is only arriving now, and is restricted to just the newest Apple Watch models. Enjoy it! To add a step counter to your watch face, long-press on the clock screen to edit it, tap on a complication (that’s what Apple calls those little icons and numbers that appear on some watch faces), choose Activity, and then tap Steps.

You don’t need this creepy feature listening in to everything, but it can be nice to have it as a backup on occasion. A button in your Apple Watch’s Control Center can turn the feature on and off. Keep it off except when you have a structured conversation that you’ll want to refer to later. This feature is currently in beta (which you can try now if you want to), but is expected to be available to everyone later this year.

It's worth turning off the default setting not just because of the creepiness factor, but also because the recaps work best when there is a single subject of conversation, with a clear start and end, and just one context. If you leave recaps running all the time, your doctor’s appointment will get mixed in with your grocery shopping, YouTube watching, and everyday chatter.

To finish off a recap and make it useful, take a look at the recap shortly after the conversation, tap the three-dots menu, and hit Edit. You’ll be able to adjust the notes and add your own important details. Siri won’t identify speakers and seems to shy away from including certain details, like people’s names. You can add in what it missed and also create your own bullet points so that everything gets noted down while it’s still fresh in your mind.

This one isn’t specific to the Series 12, but if you haven’t gotten on board with the pinch and wrist flick gestures yet, now is a great time.

First, the wrist flick: If a notification is on your screen, or you’re otherwise looking at something you’d rather be done with, just flick your wrist away from you and then back toward you, as if there were a crumb on the watch face and you wanted to knock it off. This will bring you back to the watch face and close whatever you were looking at.

The double pinch is another useful one, although Apple calls it double tap. This is confusing because you aren’t double tapping the watch, you’re tapping your thumb and forefinger together while wearing the watch. You don’t need to touch the watch face at all. So, when you get a notification or a call, look at it on your watch, and pinch your thumb and forefinger (of the watch hand) together twice. The watch detects the pinch from subtle movements in your wrist, and it will open the notification. You can then use the wrist flick to close the notification. Performing a double pinch when no notification is on screen will bring up your smart stack. You can then double-pinch to move to the next card in the smart stack, or single-pinch to open that card and see its details.

If you want to learn even more gestures, go into the Watch app, and select Accessibility and then Hand gestures. You can remap a whole-fist “clench” to do the same thing as pressing the digital crown, for example, or to open the control center or Siri.

A little rude, perhaps, but helpful: With the new AI-based Siri, sometimes answers to questions can be long-winded. If Siri launches into a novel-length response and you’re not interested in hearing all that, just put your palm over the screen. You’ll instantly be transported back to your watch face, and the Siri response will stop.

If you still want to see those longer responses without having Siri read the whole thing to you, you can set this up on your phone, and the settings will carry over to your watch. On your iPhone, go to Settings and tap Siri, then Responses. Select Silent responses instead of Spoken responses. You can then read through her answers, or skim them, as you prefer.

#3583. Short Film ‘Lightning Bug’ Gives Stage and Screen Legend Lois Smith One of Her Greatest Roles — Watch It Here

A smoke break at the Signature Theatre ultimately resulted in one of Lois Smith‘s most fascinating performances. The Tony Award winner met Zane Pais while they were both grabbing a quick cigarette while rehearsing plays. Pais had been an admirer of Smith’s work in stage productions like “The Inheritance” and films such as “Marjorie Prime” and “Five Easy Pieces,” and longed to collaborate.

“She has the most amazing delivery of lines; she’s always able to do something so unexpected with the language,” Pais said during a recent Zoom interview with Smith. “I’ve seen Lois my whole life in so many amazing shows, just be so unbelievably present on stage and be such a generous actor, and just give these heartfelt and unexpected performances. I’m a big fucking fan.” Related Stories Is A24 Finally Big Enough to Be Considered a Major Studio? Bill Hader’s Feature Directorial Debut ‘They Know’ Lands at Black Bear

So Pais wrote a short film, “Lightning Bug,” with Smith in mind. In it, she plays Lydia, a fiercely independent nonagenarian who is being pressured into selling the family home by her son and granddaughter. But things take an unexpected turn when a strange young man crashes their dinner, giving Lydia a chance to demonstrate she hasn’t missed a step despite her advanced age.

“It was all there in the script,” Smith, who recently turned 96, said. “It wasn’t complex for me to pull it off even though the script is complex.”

The role did require Smith to perform some fight choreography, but she seemed more nervous about singing a song on screen.

“I really worried: Am I going to be able to do this?” Smith said. “They made me a tape, and I listened to it and listened to it and practiced. I was nervous, but it went all right.”

“Lightning Bug” filmed over a weekend in the upstate New York home of one of Pais’s relatives. It was true no-frills, all-hands effort. The cast and crew bunked in an Airbnb, and a friend of Pais’s cooked meals for everyone.

“It felt like we were part of a theater troupe,” Pais said. “We’d work hard. Then in the evenings, we would have red wine and smoke cigarettes.”

“I seldom smoke,” Smith interjected. “Occasionally, I’ll smoke other people’s cigarettes.”

#3582. 10 Hacks Every watchOS 27 User Should Know

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

watchOS 27 introduces a solid set of upgrades to your wrist—assuming your Apple Watch supports it. While the newest update isn't Apple's most feature-filled, it does include a number of changes that improve the way you exercise, track your health, and locate missing items. That's especially true for anyone with the latest Series 12 or Ultra 4. If your Apple Watch supports watchOS 27, you should know about these 10 hacks:

With watchOS 27, Apple changed what double-pressing the Digital Crown does. Instead of opening the app switcher, it now triggers Audio Intelligence—if you have an Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4. If you don't have access to those features, the gesture now does nothing.

It seems Apple realized the mistake, however, as evidenced by watchOS 27.2. When you're using an app while running this latest update, press and hold the bottom part of the watch's screen, and you'll trigger the app switcher. You can now jump to a different app, or close an app that isn't working. Sadly, this only works when you're already in an app, and not when you're on the Home Screen, but it's certainly better than nothing.

While you can load up multiple complications on your Apple Watch, they aren't exactly dynamic. That's why I'm a big fan of the Smart Stack widgets on the Apple Watch, which update dynamically to show contextual information. Now, with the new Siri Modular Face, you can access dynamic widgets on the Home Screen. If you've just parked your car, for example, you'll see a widget showing its location; likewise, if you have an upcoming calendar appointment, it will be front and center.

To use the Siri Modular watch face, tap and hold on the screen, go to the end of the list, tap the Plus button, and find and add the Siri Modular watch face. Once you do, you'll start seeing dynamic widgets when you wake up your watch. Don't expect much personalization from this watch face, however. You can customize the colors and add three small complications, but that's it.

The double-tap gesture is one of my favorite Apple Watch features. By tapping your thumb and index finger together twice, you can do things like answer a call or reply to a message. In watchOS 27, Apple took the gesture one step forward. You can now use the double-tap gesture to scroll through your widgets; if you perform a single tap, it then opens the highlighted widget or the shortcut. This means you can open and browse the weather app, or start a workout, without ever touching your Apple Watch's screen.

Your Apple Watch's new Music Recognition app has native Shazam integration. What's more, Shazam will record your request even when you're offline and away from your iPhone. The moment you reconnect, the service will identify the songs, which you can see in the Shazam app on your iPhone or Apple Watch.

It seems like Apple has a library of songs it uses for offline recognition, because in my testing, it was able to recognize a Coldplay song instantly, even when in Airplane mode. To use it, you can either open the Music Recognition app, or you can add the widget for faster access. Scroll up on the Home Screen, go to the bottom of the screen, tap the Edit button, then the Plus button, and add the Music Recognition widget.

Apple Watches have traditionally lacked a live step count widget or complication. To find your step count, you had to go to the bottom of the Activity app, or rely on third-party apps. But even still, these apps never showed live data. You’d always have to wait a couple of seconds to see the updated stats.

Now, if you own the latest Apple Watch Series 12 or the Ultra 4, you can add a live step count widget or complication to the Apple Watch face or the Smart Stack. This will show you your precise step count at all times. To use it, go to the bottom of the Smart Stack, tap the Edit button, then tap the Plus button. Here, find and add the new Step count widget.

Siri is no longer a voice assistant that you use for one-off tasks. With Siri AI, you can now carry on multiple conversations with context and memory. It's not as robust as ChatGPT or Claude, but you can use Siri AI for brainstorming, researching, and jotting down ideas for later.

The Siri AI app on the iPhone shows all your conversations, and so does the Apple Watch. This means you can continue your Siri AI conversations and view past chats on your Apple Watch. To use it, press the Digital Crown once, then tap the Siri app icon in the center. This will open up all your conversations instead of calling upon Siri. Tap a conversation to continue your chat on the Apple Watch. Of course, anything you do here will be reflected in the Siri app on your iPhone.

The new Find My app on the Apple Watch shows a single map for finding people, devices, and items. This means you can now locate your family members who are sharing their location with you, as well as AirTags or other Find My items from the watchOS app.

After opening the app, you can use the Digital Crown to zoom in or out of the map. Use touch to pan around. The map doesn't show all items and people at once, though. Tap the Menu button at the bottom-right corner, and then switch between People, Items, or Devices. If you have multiple items, you can scroll through them using the Digital Crown.

While it's not a Whoop-level feature, the Apple Watch now includes a Readiness score. Instead of individually looking at your training load, sleep score, and vitals, you now have one number that gives you the whole picture.

The Readiness score ranges from 0 to 10 and is based on your recent fitness activity, sleep data, and background health monitoring. If you have a score of 8 to 10, your Apple Watch thinks you can push yourself, or "go for it," as it says; if it's below 5, the watch thinks you should consider lighter activity. This feature, though, is only available on Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. You can use the new Readiness app on your Apple Watch to see this data, but you can also access it on your iPhone in the Fitness app's new Readiness section.

Low Power Mode isn't your only option when it comes to extending the battery life for your Apple Watch. watchOS 27 offers a special Max Extended Workout mode just for long workouts. With it, your Apple Watch disables some features, like splits and alerts, and reduces the frequency of GPS and heart rate readings, in the hopes of extending your battery throughout your entire exercise. To use it, go to the Workout app and select the workout you want. Tap the Goals button in the top-right corner, and choose the Extended option. Then, switch to the Max Extended option and start your workout.

The Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 come with a set of Audio Intelligence features that use the microphones on the Apple Watch, paired with AI models (both local and cloud-based), to identify sounds, music, and record conversation. Thanks to this new feature, one of the iPhone's accessibility features also makes its way to the Apple Watch.

Sound Recognition can alert you when it hears sirens, alarms, doorbells, and more, even when your iPhone isn’t around. To set this up, go to the Settings app on your iPhone and navigate to Accessibility > Sound & Name Recognition > Sound Recognition. Here, enable the sounds you want to monitor, and make sure to turn on the Detect using Apple Watch toggle.

#3581. GTA 6 Players Are Officially Spending an ‘Absolutely Bonkers’ Amount of Time with the Game

Launch day playtime stats for Grand Theft Auto 6 are off the charts

Grand Theft Auto 6 players weren't kidding about wanting to spend the game's entire launch day in Leonida. Much hullabaloo was made about people requesting time off from work or faking sick to spend the entire day playing GTA 6, and plenty of companies tried to capitalize on that conversation with marketing stunts.

Mat Piscatella, senior director at market research firm Circana, shared data on Friday about just how much time players spent with GTA 6 on its launch day, Thursday, Nov. 19. "PS5 GTA VI players averaged 513 minutes that day, Xbox players 494," he said in a post on Bluesky. That's an average of 8.55 and 8.23 hours for PS5 and Xbox players, respectively. That means GTA 6 players effectively spent the length of a workday stealing drugs, beating up rednecks, driving around Fake Florida, kicking bodega cats, and playing GTA 6's in-game video games.

You could fly from New York City to Seattle in under 8.55 hours. You could watch the entirety of the original Star Wars trilogy in under 8.55 hours. You could binge The Office season 4 in under 8.55 hours. You could finish Resident Evil 2 in under 8.55 hours, and probably still have enough time to finish it again. You could get an honest-to-god good night's sleep for under 8.55 hours, on average. All I'm saying is, 8.55 hours is a long time, especially for an average.

The average playtime stat is certainly eye-catching, but other numbers Piscatella shared are perhaps even more staggering. 61% of US-based PlayStation 5 players and 56% of global Xbox Series X players "engaged" with GTA 6 on its launch day, figures Piscatella called "absolutely bonkers." He used Fortnite to put that in perspective: Epic Games' battle royale was the second-most played game on Nov. 19 with 10% of PlayStation and Xbox players engaging with it.

Those numbers are as unbelievable as GTA 6's sales figures. According to Take-Two Interactive, GTA 6's launch is now the biggest entertainment launch in history with $3.79 billion generated in revenue.

#3580. Walter Hill on Sam Peckinpah, Steve McQueen, and His Revolutionary Screenplay for ‘The Getaway’

In 1972, Walter Hill was a young screenwriter with just one produced movie (“Hickey & Boggs”) behind him when he scored an enviable gig: adapting Jim Thompson’s tough-as-nails crime novel “The Getaway” for actor/producer Steve McQueen (then one of the biggest movie stars in the world) and director Sam Peckinpah (then, as now, one of the greatest directors who ever lived). On Wednesday night, Hill spoke before a packed screening at the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures and looked back on the movie that jump-started not only his screenwriting endeavors, but a directing career that would ultimately include classics like “The Warriors,” “48hrs.,” and “Streets of Fire.” Related Stories Short Film ‘Lightning Bug’ Gives Stage and Screen Legend Lois Smith One of Her Greatest Roles — Watch It Here Is A24 Finally Big Enough to Be Considered a Major Studio?

“The Getaway” screened as part of the museum’s “Branch Selects” series, in which the Academy’s various branches program films they feel exemplify their crafts. “The Getaway” was, appropriately enough, selected by the writers branch, and screenwriter and Academy Governor Larry Karaszewski was on hand to introduce the movie and moderate the pre-screening discussion with Hill. Karaszewski, a longtime “Getaway” enthusiast who carried newspaper ads from the movie around in his wallet when he was 10 years old, pointed out that Hill changed the entire architecture of screenwriting when he burst onto the scene in the early 1970s.

“ Walter, right off the bat, changed the art of screenwriting,” Karaszewski said. “We have an award show here at the Oscars called the Sci-Tech Awards, where they give awards to things that silently change the industry and advance them into the future. I really feel that Walter Hill did that in screenwriting, but it wasn’t a technical advancement. It was a literary advancement. He changed what a page should look like as a screenplay and what it could feel like to read it.” Karaszewski went on to illustrate his point by projecting pages from Robert Bolt’s “Doctor Zhivago” screenplay and Walter Hill’s “Hard Times” side by side on the screen.

“You don’t even have to read [Bolt’s script], just look at it,” Karaszewski said, pointing out the dense blocks of words compared to Hill’s lean, spare page. “You’re looking at monoliths. It’s dense, and there are camera moves and references to things you would never see on screen. Walter Hill taught screenwriters that you can strip all that away. You can still direct on the page, but not by calling for specific camera movements — just by saying what you’re seeing. Walter’s scripts are made out of short sentences and white space. He looked at the placement of each line as part of the storytelling. He turned the carriage return into an art form.”

As Karaszewski welcomed Hill to the stage, he pointed out that “The Getaway” — a smart, terse tale of a couple (Steve McQueen and Ali MacGraw) on the run after their involvement in a botched bank robbery — represented the emergence of Hill’s developing voice. “You’ll already see the beginnings of that remarkable style, the economy, the precision, the sense that every line is pushing you toward the next image.” Yet, as Hill revealed in his lively conversation with Karaszewski, the ruthless efficiency of the pacing and the concentrated emotional impact of “The Getaway” were not easily arrived at.

“I think it’s much harder to adapt than it is to write an original, which is the reverse of the normal theory,” Hill said. “With an original, it’s just you at your desk with the typewriter or pen. When you’re adapting, that almost always means that somebody else owns it, so you’re not simply writing based on your own opinions about what should be in and what should be out, but there’s the producer’s opinion, and the studio’s, and the actor’s. There were all these political currents that one had to navigate.”

One such political current came from megastar McQueen, who didn’t interfere much with Hill’s writing but did have one caveat that amused the screenwriter. “He wanted to play a reasonably sympathetic outlaw,” Hill said. “That was not in the Thompson sensibility. So we already had a disparity, but the producer wanted to keep Steve happy.”

“The Getaway” began as an assignment not for Peckinpah, but for Peter Bogdanovich, who was white-hot coming off of successes like “The Last Picture Show” and “What’s Up, Doc?” Bogdanovich didn’t last long, however, given his clashes with McQueen and McQueen’s power as the film‘s star. “I couldn’t imagine two more diverse sensibilities than Steve and Peter,” Hill said, noting that he had his own disagreements with Bogdanovich over the movie’s tone but wasn’t in a position to argue. “You’ve got to remember, I was nobody. I had one screen credit. And these were big players.”

The big players included not only Bogdanovich and McQueen, but MacGraw, hot off of the smash hit “Love Story.” MacGraw was pushed into the movie by her husband, Paramount studio chief Robert Evans, which Hill found amusing given the way everything played out. “I’m going to tread lightly here,” Hill said of the behind-the-scenes melodrama involving MacGraw leaving Evans when she fell in love with McQueen. “When the material was optioned and I was hired, Bob saw the movie as a fabulous idea for Steve and Ali. It didn’t work out so well for him.”

After Bogdanovich and McQueen butted heads, Bogdanovich was let go and Peckinpah, who McQueen had enjoyed working with on “Junior Bonner,” came in to take his place. “We were very lucky to get such a talented guy, obviously,” Hill said. “I thought of him then and I think of him now as one of the great directors with a very unique sensibility. I was very privileged to work with him — which doesn’t mean he and I agreed about everything.”

Hill’s biggest disagreement with Peckinpah had to do with a scene in which MacGraw’s character considered killing McQueen before turning the gun on his nemesis — and the man with whom MacGraw had gone to bed to secure McQueen’s early release from prison. This was a scene carried over from the book, which was darker and more paranoid than what made it to the screen given McQueen’s mandate that he be sympathetic. Hill felt that the moment no longer worked now that the relationship between McQueen and MacGraw was softer and more relatable in the novel.

“I thought that for the movie we were trying to make, you might forgive your wife for sleeping with a bad man to do a very good thing for you,” Hill said. “That seemed to be to be conceivable. But if your wife fell into cahoots with the bad guy and actually was thinking about killing you and actually turned the gun on you before she decided to shoot the other guy…this did not track for me. But this is the screenwriter’s dilemma: you either talk the director into your point of view, or you make the change that he wants — or somebody else will. Those are your choices.”

Hill lost the argument but liked the movie Peckinpah made in the end. “He staged it beautifully,” Hill said. “He shot it beautifully. It’s got one of Steve’s best performances. And the movie turned out to be his greatest hit. He used to call me every once in a while after I became a director and say, ‘Write me another one.'” Ironically, it was the success of “The Getaway” that put Hill in a position where didn’t have to write for other directors anymore.

“Larry Gordon had a producing deal to make low-budget movies at Columbia,” Hill said. “He would give young writers a chance to direct, because he said, ‘Even if they’re no good as directors, at least we’ll get a good script. Most of the directors I’m working with aren’t any good anyway.'” Gordon gave Hill the opportunity to direct “Hard Times,” and the rest was history. Aside from kicking off Hill’s directing career, the collaboration became the first of many between the two men. “He’s a wonderful guy and a wonderful producer.”

Now in his 80s, Hill continues to write and direct (his last film was the exquisite character-driven Western “Dead for a Dollar“), plying his trade in the world of graphic novels in between film projects. “I’ve had four of them published in France,” Hill said, joking that the only one published in America was “the least good of them,” but promising another one on the way. “You’ve got to keep your hand in somehow.”

#3579. I Analyzed the Seven Biggest AI Chatbots to Determine How Safe They Are for Kids

David Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years.

He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

AI safety for both adults and children is under greater scrutiny than ever before, with a growing number of questions and concerns appearing around how beneficial or otherwise these conversational bots actually are for our mental well-being—even without considering their energy use, ethics, or economic implications. At the same time, an increasing number of apps and services are becoming age-gated in a growing number of countries around the world, as governments realize that letting kids loose on AI apps, social media platforms, and the web at large might not be the best idea for their ongoing development and prosperity.

The big AI apps, such as ChatGPT and Gemini, are right in the center of these trends, and the companies behind them are taking steps that they promise will keep children safe. If you want to know what youngsters in your family may be getting exposed to, and what you can do about it, here's the rundown.

OpenAI's ChatGPT has one of the more comprehensive setups in terms of parental controls. The minimum age for users is 13, and if you're under 18, you need to have parental consent to open an account—age is predicted via several signals, including what times of day you use ChatGPT and what you talk about.

Accounts for under-18s automatically become ChatGPT for Teens accounts. There's more of a focus on learning and study (with a dedicated study mode), as well as "age-appropriate safeguards to help reduce exposure to sensitive or potentially harmful content." There are built-in protections for "harmful topics," including sexual, romantic, or violent roleplay, graphic violence, and self-harm. These work on top of the safeguards for all users that limit chats about physical harm and illegal activity.

These ChatGPT for Teens accounts can also be linked to a parental account—but while parental consent is required for under-18s to use the service, ChatGPT clearly says that teens do have the option to break the link if they want. If you do persuade your kid to keep your accounts connected, you can set time limits on when the AI bot can be used, and tweak some of the sensitivity settings. However, you can't view any conversations.

To set up parental controls from ChatGPT on the web, click your profile icon (bottom left), then Settings > Parental controls > Add family member and follow the instructions. It's also worth bearing in mind that ChatGPT app can also be used for free, anonymously, in any web browser, though OpenAI says users accessing the AI this way are subject to the default under-18s limits (and can't save chats or access an archive).

Gemini is tied into everything else Google does, and follows the broader rules for Google accounts: No under-13s, unless you're part of a family group and using an account managed by an adult. You can manage your family through the Family Link portal on the web, though as far as parental controls specific to Gemini go, you can only enable or disable access to the AI (settings like screen time apply across all enabled apps).

For all under-18s (partly identified through age estimation), whether or not they're part of a managed family group, Google applies some additional protections. They include preventing the AI from taking on a persona, guarding against emotional dependence on the AI, and discouraging bullying and other forms of harassment. There are also safeguards to limit chats about age-restricted substances like alcohol or vapes, and mental health issues like eating disorders.

These protections for minors are applied in addition to the usual guardrails in Gemini for everyone. The guardrails should lead you away from conversations about self-harm, suicide, violence, and illegal activities, and offer quick links to support in times of crisis. However, Google itself admits that these filters aren't perfect.

As with ChatGPT, there's a loophole of sorts in that anyone can start chatting with Gemini, for free inside a web browser, with no checks at all. These conversations can't be saved and come up against usage limits fairly quickly, but they're only protected by the general restrictions for all accounts, not the ones specific to minors.

Meta AI will show up in several apps that young people and children are likely to use, including WhatsApp and Instagram, as well as having its own separate app on the web and on phones. The standard restrictions for Meta's social media accounts apply to its AI too: A minimum age of 13, and restrictions for all under-18s. Like many other platforms, it uses some AI magic to flag up accounts being used by minors.

If you're under 18 and on a Meta Teen account, you'll come up against blocks if you try to get Meta AI to engage in sexual or romantic roleplay, or discuss alcohol or substance misuse. Chats on topics such as eating disorders and self-harm will prompt the AI to offer guidance towards relevant support services.

Meta offers a comprehensive parental control setup for its apps, including Meta AI, but connecting a parent account isn't compulsory for teens. This is handled through the Meta Family Center portal, and parents can get reports on the general topics that kids are chatting about with AI—though they don't get the exact transcripts or prompts. Any self-harm or suicide discussion can trigger an alert to the connected parent account.

All users, under 18 or over 18, get support and crisis intervention responses when chatting about suicide and self-harm, and there are strict limits on discussing illegal and harmful acts, including drug use and cyberbullying, as well as sexual and adult content.

Apple users have to be 13 or over to have an account, which is required to access Siri AI—anyone younger needs to have an account created for them by an adult, and these accounts can only get at the basic, older Siri. Date of birth must be declared when opening an Apple account, with tighter checks rolling out in many parts of the world.

Anyone over the age of 13 can have an Apple account and use the Siri AI app, with or without a connected parent account, as it stands in most U.S. states. This means the well-being safeguards are essentially the same for teens as they are for adults: There are safeguards around self-harm, suicide, sexual and violent content, and illegal commands. It's one of the more conservative AIs when it comes to what it will talk about.

The new and improved Siri AI can be managed to some extent by the new parental controls available in iOS 27 and Apple's other software updates for 2026—Apple has clearly seen the way the wind is blowing—but this is optional for teens. It depends on whether or not you can corral your kids into a Family Sharing group.

If your teens are in your family group of users, then the standard Screen Time rules apply for controlling app usage limits and device access (in iOS Settings, tap your name, then Family to get at them). There are also options for disabling certain Siri AI features, such as the writing tools or the image creation capabilities.

Like Gemini/Google and Apple/Siri, Copilot is tied into the wider Microsoft ecosystem, and access for under-18s can be managed through it. Users must be 13 or older to hold a Microsoft or a Copilot account—and again, there's some underlying tech in place to detect anyone who might be deliberately lying about their age.

If you've got a teen using Copilot, you can manage their access through the standard Microsoft Family Safety portal. You're able to enable or disable Copilot access, set times during which Copilot can and can't be used, and disable certain features like image generation or voice mode. Parents can't read the Copilot chats of their kids, though.

Parental supervision is optional—a teen aged 13–17 can use Copilot without linking their account to an adult one. Microsoft says users identified as under 18 won't see personalized results or ads, and will get age-appropriate responses regarding risky or harmful content, though there's not much detail on what that entails.

More generally, content around self-harm, violence, adult content, harassment, and harmful or illegal activity is banned on the AI platform. Any prompts about suicide or drugs will bring up support options rather than answers, whether you're an adult or a young person using the service.

Out of the bigger AI chatbots out there, Grok is very much the worst at protecting minors. It can be accessed through X or as its own standalone app, and while its terms of use indicate there's a minimum age requirement of 13, a recent report by Common Sense Media says the platform's age checks aren't effective.

Ultimately that means that minors have the same access to Grok as adults, if they want it—an AI platform that combines "weak safety guardrails" and "a range of extremely harmful content" that includes "explicit sexual content, mental health risks, violent content, and inappropriate responses to... offensive content" (that's the Common Sense Media Report again).

Yes, this is the AI chatbot that has previously had a problem with deepfake porn imagery, and which has traditionally taken a rather casual attitude towards safety concerns, led by SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk. While illegal and harmful content is supposedly banned from Grok, its own FAQs admit that certain chats can result in "dialogue that may involve coarse language, crude humor, sexual situations, or violence."

There is actually a Grok Kids Mode that limits the kind of content that can be shown and the conversation topics that can be added, but it requires users to self-declare themselves as minors and is easy to bypass. The advice from Common Sense Media seems to be the way to go with Grok: Do not let your teens access it.

Claude's approach to child safety is straightforward: You can only register for an account if you're over 18. It is possible to lie about your age when signing up, but like the other platforms, Anthropic looks at various "signals" in behavior to spot minors—if your account gets flagged, you have to verify your age using an option like face age estimation or Yoti.

There's no free web access to the chatbot, like there is with ChatGPT and Gemini, so if you're under 18, you're locked out from the service unless you know the behavioral tricks to get past Claude's detection systems.

In terms of more general well-being protections on Claude, any chat around self-harm or suicide will guide users towards helplines and other resources for support. Conversations about illegal activities, disallowed speech, and explicit sexual content are banned from the platform. In recent months, Anthropic says it's also reduced AI sycophancy.

That's something of a whistle-stop tour of the big seven AI chatbots, but if you're a parent, it should give you some idea of what's out there and how easy it is to access. Besides the parental controls built into these AIs (or not), you also have the settings available at the platform level—Android, iOS, Windows, macOS—to restrict the use of any potentially harmful apps.

#3578. 9 Video Game Sequels Better Than the Original

In theory, sequels should always be better than the original since it is easier to see the flaws of the first and correct them. However, sometimes it’s too difficult to capture the certain magic that the first title had, and this is especially true for video games like The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild. However, that isn’t always true, with some sequels not only living up to the hype, but also becoming better video games.

That is why this list will feature eight video game sequels that are better than the original based on aspects such as improvements, design, gameplay, narrative, originality, fan opinion, critical acclaim, and overall quality. These games took the base of something great and made it even better, becoming the definitive version and a sequel that improved on almost everything. Please note that Red Dead Redemption 2 will not be on this list because it is a prequel, not a sequel.

Games on this list don’t specifically need to be the second game in a franchise, as long as they are a sequel, which opens the door for Baldur’s Gate 3. When the player is infected by a Mind Flayer parasite, they will turn into one if they don’t find a cure for themselves. Teaming up with others in their position, gamers travel across the country in search of this concoction, but the brewing war between gods and mortals makes this much more complicated.

Baldur’s Gate 3 is the most recent game on this list, but it didn’t take long to become one of the most influential titles of all time. This is the ultimate role-playing experience, improving on the narrative, scale, gameplay, graphics, and options. Baldur’s Gate 3 is as good a sequel as it can get, even if this entire franchise is home to masterpieces. There is so much love and passion put into this game, and fans can feel it in every ounce of the design, which is exactly what every sequel should have.

Batman is one of the biggest superheroes of all time, with his presence extending from comics to movies and even video games. Batman: Arkham City puts Bruce Wayne into the titular prison, which is a walled-off section of Gotham City. Donning the cap and cowl, players must learn of Protocol 10, the mysterious plan Hugo Strange has set, but first, Batman needs to take care of the many villains trying to kill him.

Batman: Arkham Asylum is a fantastic game, but most fans will agree the sequel is much better. The open-world allowed for more engaging traversal, the narrative was tenser and had fewer errors, and the gameplay was extended with more combos, making it one of the best martial arts video games. It is the perfect follow-up to an already incredible video game, arguably establishing itself as the definitive Batman experience not just in video games, but overall.

Resident Evil is celebrating its 30th anniversary in 2026, with massive projects such as Resident Evil Requiem and the film directed by Zach Cregger. However, nothing can compare to Resident Evil 4, the best sequel in the franchise. When the daughter of the president is kidnapped by a cult in Spain, Leon S. Kennedy goes to save her. But when he learns the cult has been infected by a parasite, survival and escape become even more difficult.

The first Resident Evil is great, but most of the sequels are better than it, especially Resident Evil 4. While polarizing to some, the changes made in Resident Evil 4 revitalized the franchise, adding stylish action mechanics and an over-the-shoulder camera view. It was simple, but very effective, making this game way easier to play than other titles while maintaining the core difficulty and fun. Resident Evil 4 is a horror masterpiece and a sequel that is one of the best games ever.

It was recently announced that EA shut down BioWare, the game studio that brought fans so many classics, including the Mass Effect franchise. Each game is nearly perfect, but Mass Effect 2 in particular stands out as one of the best. Years after the first game, Commander Shepard is killed in the line of duty, only to be revived shortly after. Those who brought him back to life task him with investigating a mysterious alien race that has abducted entire human colonies, harvesting people to build a new threat to the entire galaxy.

The first Mass Effect was a terrific video game that established the beloved formula, and this sequel took what was great in that and expanded on it. The first bright spot is the fact that progress from the first game is saved in the sequel, creating an interconnected feel that makes decisions long-term. Mass Effect 2 strips away the original inventory management, repetitive exploration, and stiff shooting, replacing them with improved mechanics and design for a much better experience. With the gameplay greatly improved, it could then focus on what the franchise is best known for: the worldbuilding, which is what makes Mass Effect 2 one of the best sci-fi video games for beginners.

Assassin’s Creed is one of the best historical video game franchises of all time, and while it has changed its formula to be more mythological and open-world RPG, the roots of historical stealth are unmatched, and that is highlighted by Assassin’s Creed II. Set in Renaissance Italy during the late 15th century, the story follows Ezio, a young Florentine nobleman whose father and brothers are framed for treason and publicly executed. He dons his father’s assassin robes and embarks on a quest for vengeance against those who wronged him, including the Templar Order.

When it comes to superior sequels, Assassin’s Creed II is a textbook example, transforming the foundation into a player-driven experience. Adding mission variety, this mix of tasks built a much better experience in terms of gameplay, and set in the gorgeous Renaissance cities, it was a true joy to explore. Ezio is also regarded as the best protagonist in the franchise, and it isn’t hard to see why, providing a decades-spanning character arc that shows his entire evolution. Assassin’s Creed II is a complete overhaul that creates the quintessential game in the franchise.

The Witcher franchise is at an all-time high, with a TV show adaptation, new DLC, and a sequel, which all started because of the popularity of The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt. Geralt of Rivia is a Witcher, but he must put aside his usual monster-hunting gig in order to save Ciri, his adoptive daughter, from the titular spectral group that wants to use her powers for evil.

When talking about The Witcher, most fans just ignore the first two since they didn’t play them. And while they are good, they don’t hold a candle to the third game. The combat can be better, but the worldbuilding and narrative more than make up for that. Lore and details spawn in every corner of the map, with side quests starting as something simple and then evolving into a grand yet personal tale. Not to mention, monster hunting is a pure delight that forces players to be tactical, proving why it is one of the best video games of the 2010s and better than its predecessors.

Four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in return.

You belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is finding out what is over there.

You would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the people are where it all gets complicated.

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as everybody kept telling you.

Grand Theft Auto is arguably the greatest video game franchise of all time, and if there was any doubt, it disappeared after Grand Theft Auto VI came out to glowing reviews. Bringing gamers back to Vice City decades later, they control dual protagonists, Lucia and Jason, a couple who work their way through the chaotic city from common thieves to a criminal power couple.

Grand Theft Auto VI is officially the highest-rated video game of all time, meaning it is clearly better than its predecessors. While some fans will disagree, there is no denying that the hype paid off, delivering an incredibly rich world of crime, freedom, and chaos. The sheer detail in every corner of Vice City is astounding, and beyond looking gorgeous, GTA VI is the most mechanically deep in the franchise, proving why it is the definitive GTA sequel.

While the most recent Street Fighter movie was critically panned, the sequel has a good chance of being better since the original Street Fighter II is the best game in the franchise. M. Bison hosts an international fighting tournament that brings in the strongest brawlers from around the world, all competing to test their might and win the ultimate prize, but there might be some ulterior motives behind this competition.

The fighting genre, as gamers know it, was built on the back of Street Fighter II, which not only improved the franchise but gaming as a whole. The added combo system became a staple in virtually every game going forward, and the improved graphics, controls, and combat variants made gameplay infinitely more engaging. There aren't many fighting games better than Street Fighter II; it's just a pity the franchise peaked this early.

Valve is one of the greatest video game studios ever, and it seems they have a knack for sequels, with a couple of masterpieces, such as Half-Life 2 and Portal 2. The latter is set years after the first, with Chell waking up to the same facility, except this time it is falling apart. Working with a friendly robot, she attempts to escape the facility, but the reawakening of GLaDOS makes this more challenging.

Portal 2 is an amazing game from start to finish that takes the base of the first game and builds something entirely new on top of it. This game makes the first look like a vertical slice because of the sheer details, expanded gameplay, narrative, and scale. The co-op mode also offers a fun multiplayer experience and new ways to play. Portal 2 isn’t just better than the first game, but it may be the greatest game of all time.

#3577. GTA 6: Why You Shouldn’t Keep Your Money In Jason’s House

When you first get started in Grand Theft Auto 6, Jason isn't exactly the most fiscally responsible person, and one of the first things you learn is that he's been keeping his money underneath the floorboards in his bedroom. Throughout the first chapter, you can actually deposit money into the floorboard stash anytime, and up until you open up your BuckMe account, this is really the only means of storing your money. However, players who are putting away a ton of cash in Jason's house are in for a rude awakening.

!!! WARNING: THIS GUIDE CONTAINS SPOILERS FOR CHAPTER 2 OF GRAND THEFT AUTO 6 !!!

Without giving too many story details away, players will essentially start Chapter 2 with almost no money due to the climactic ending of Chapter 1. If you're wondering where all the money went that you'd been storing in Jason's floorboards, I've got bad news for you: it's all gone.

You can return to Jason's house at the start of Chapter 2, but any money you deposited in the floorboard safe will no longer be there. It's a major blow that players likely won't be expecting, and if you've been planning on spending that money later down the road, the story is designed in a way that you really won't be able to recover those funds.

Instead of depositing money into the floorboards at Jason's house, my advice is to invest as much money as you can during Chapter 1 into upgrades, gear, etc., and max out your BuckMe family savings account. Any money you don't spend will essentially be lost when you start Chapter 2, and the story is largely rooted in Lucia and Jason starting from scratch and climbing their way back from the bottom by doing odd jobs across Leonida.

That said, starting in Chapter 2, you will finally be able to claim the "Rainy Day Funds" envelope that's under the floorboards at Jason's house. This is, of course, a separate stash of money than the cash you earned and deposited there during Chapter 1, and was unaffected by the events of Chapter 2's conclusion despite the cash sitting right next to it being lost.

The "Rainy Day Fund" envelope contains $5000 and will come in very useful at the start of Chapter 2, but getting to Jason's house from the motel in Chapter 2 is quite a trek. Additionally, you'll be able to collect the family photos of Lucia and Jason that were in the box, and if you were worried about Lucia and Jason's pet snake Delores, she's safe and sound under the stairs and is sitting on a little surprise as well.

Further, if you're planning to return to Jason's house early in Grand Theft Auto 6 Chapter 2, note that it's heavily guarded by police and you'll need to use stealth in order to claim the "Rainy Day Fund" envelope. If you're being chased or alert the police, they'll shoot on site and you will not be able to grab the money or pictures.

#3576. How to Check Your Flight Status After the FAA Canceled the Ground Stop for All Airports

Update, 8:41 p.m.: The Federal Aviation Administration announced it has ended the ground stop.

On Friday afternoon, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a nationwide ground stop for all airports in the United States. If you're planning to fly this afternoon or evening, or you have friends or family doing the same, you're likely concerned about tracking flight statuses. While there's still a lot we don't know, there are tools to help track flights at this time:

There are a number of options for tracking flights, whether you have your flight number or not. If you have the flight number, the fastest method is to Google it: Google will display a live tracker of your flight at the top of the results page. You can also head to the airline's official website to track your flight: United Airlines, for example, has a flight tracker where you can either enter your route information or your flight number. Most, if not all, airlines will have a similar tool you can use.

Alternatively, you can use a site or service that tracks all flights. FlightAware is one such site and has a flight tracker that lets you search flights—so long as you know the origin and the destination. If you have the flight number, your iPhone can help: You can enter your flight number into Spotlight search to see a live tracker, or you can text a contact your flight number, then tap the link that appears under the number to see a tracker of the flight.

At this time, the exact reason isn't totally clear. According to the agency, “The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following communication issues impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers,” but the FAA hasn't said what caused those communications issues or when they expect to lift the grounding. The grounding order comes one day after a massive Microsoft outage that disrupted service for users of Outlook, Teams, and other Microsoft products. It also comes one day after Ars Technica reported that the FAA was rolling out an AI-powered tool to help manage air traffic across the country.

This is only the third time in U.S. history that the FAA has made such an order—once after 9/11, and again in January of 2023 due to a pilot alert system issue; the latter ground stop lasted around 90 minutes.

#3575. ‘Josephine’ Review: Another Heartsick Horror Film About Real Monsters from ‘Soft & Quiet’ Filmmaker

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on January 23, 2026 during the 2026 Sundance Film Festival. Sumerian Pictures will release the film in limited theaters on Friday, November 20, with a wide release to follow on Friday, December 4.]

At this point, filmmaker Beth de Araújo is two for two. Not just in terms of the quality of her films — impeccably crafted fever dreams of very different stripes and horrifyingly similar themes — but in how these films make the viewer feel.

More concisely: with her “Soft & Quiet” and “Josephine,” de Araújo remains undefeated when it comes to making stunning films that I will both heartily recommend and never, ever watch again. Related Stories Walter Hill on Sam Peckinpah, Steve McQueen, and His Revolutionary Screenplay for ‘The Getaway’ Short Film ‘Lightning Bug’ Gives Stage and Screen Legend Lois Smith One of Her Greatest Roles — Watch It Here

The word that comes to mind when watching a de Araújo feature is heartsick. That applies to the feeling bestowed on both the audience and her characters (the good guys and the bad guys). While her first film, the unrelenting “Soft & Quiet,” was cleverly designed to appear as if it was shot in a single real-time take, her sophomore feature is more about the steady accumulation of dread. The heroines of “Soft & Quiet” recognize what they are dealing with almost immediately (the force of the evil that is bent on destroying them is what’s surprises most), but the star at the center of “Josephine” is not just wounded by the sickness that suddenly infiltrates her young life, but her complete lack of understanding about what is happening to her and why.

In both films, it’s not just bad deeds that upends everyday lives, it’s real evil, actual monsters, perversions that don’t only show up in a movie screen. That’s true terror.

Based loosely on an experience de Araújo, who both wrote and directed the film, experienced as a child, “Josephine” initially lulls us into a false sense of safety. It’s early morning in San Francisco, and fledgling soccer star Josephine (Mason Reeves, riveting in her first role) is getting ready for a run with her devoted dad Damien (Channing Tatum, bringing incredible girl-dad energy to the role). It’s something the pair do every Sunday morning: get up early to watch Premier League football, run through a woodsy neighboring park, and kick the ball around.

For her second film, de Araújo leans less on clever camera tricks, though she and cinematographer Greta Zozula occasionally put us in Josephine’s own perspective, shooting as if we are looking through the eight-year-old’s eyes. As with “Soft & Quiet,” the gimmick works, grounding us in Josephine’s world and immersing us, if briefly, in what the world looks like from her vantage. Jo-Jo, as her dad calls her, is plucky and fun and filled with energy, so when she briefly zips ahead of her dad while on their run through Golden Gate Park, it just seems like everyday high-jinks.

But when the path forks (about as heavy-handed a metaphor as de Araújo will ever employ), Josephine goes to the left, while Damien goes to the right. What she finds there will forever alter the course of her life, and set “Josephine” off on a heart-wrenching journey with no easy answers. Curious and watchful, Josephine ducks behind a tree when she sees a woman (Syra McCarthy) running into a public bathroom at the bottom of a scrubby hill, and she sinks even further down when a young man (a bone-chilling Philip Ettinger) follows the unknown woman into the tiny building.

De Araújo’s approach to portraying on-screen violence only furthers that heartsick feeling: straightforward, unsparing, and absolutely devoid of any possibility of being compared to “torture porn.” What we see, what Josephine sees, is something no person should ever witness or experience. And that’s the root of the film’s power: how do we talk about things that we should not have words for?

When Damien arrives on the scene, it kicks off what will become one of Tatum’s best performances yet, a deep-feeling and heartbreaking exploration of layers of emotional unease. Damien does everything “right,” ensuring both Josephine and the woman are safe, chasing after the assailant, calling the cops, a neat little checklist of “how to handle an emergency.” And yet, the damage has already been done. There will be more to come.

Even when Josephine begins to seek out answers to what she’s seen (snatching her mom’s phone to search “raip,” reeling at what she discovers), it’s impossible to make sense of everything. There are things to fear she never even know existed, and the deep-seated powerlessness that overtakes her causes her to act out in chilling and increasingly volatile ways. Her parents’ reactions don’t help: her exceedingly calm mother Claire (Gemma Chan, thrilling as a character just barely holding it together) wants her to see a therapist now, her more action-oriented dad is eager to put her into self-defense classes. The mixed messages both give off (to say nothing of their own barely concealed terror) do little to help Josephine, who soon becomes someone almost entirely different than the care-free kid she just was.

She also picks up a new friend: Ettinger begins to appear to her, a literal haunting figure, never saying a word, yet barging into nearly every moment of Josephine’s already upended life. It’s the sort of choice another filmmaker fight fill tricksy or silly, but that de Araújo delivers with the maximum of impact. And that we, like Josephine and only Josephine, can see him only furthers our immersion into her world. It almost goes beyond empathy.

Josephine’s steadily unfolding breakdown is only compounded by the arrival of yet another situation no eight-year-old should ever have to encounter: handling the messy investigation of the crime itself. How she might help (or not) drives one more wedge between Josephine and her parents, who all have a different take on what the “right” thing to do is.

If these questions sound heady and heavy, they are, but de Araújo’s masterful ability to interrogate tension on every level keeps the film clipping along, each turn both a surprise and an inevitability. The monsters are here, they are real, and they’re coming.

“Josephine” premiered at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival.
